title: Enhanced coherence of rare-earth nuclear spins in a crystal
summary: Rare-earth ions in crystals are useful in precision measurements and quantum information science because of their exceptional optical and spin coherence properties. We show that the nuclear spin coherence time of $^{153}\mathrm{Eu}^{3+}$ ions doped into yttrium orthosilicate can be significantly enhanced by driving the $^{89}\mathrm{Y}$ nuclear spins in the host crystal. This improvement in spin coherence time opens up ways to improve the precision of measurements using rare-earth-doped crystals.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that driving the 89Y nuclear spins in the host crystal yttrium orthosilicate significantly enhances the nuclear spin coherence time of 153Eu3+ ions doped into it, which improves precision measurement capabilities using rare-earth-doped crystals.
AI.motivation: Rare-earth ions in crystals are valuable for precision measurements and quantum information science due to their exceptional optical and spin coherence properties, and enhancing their coherence times can further improve measurement precision.
AI.method: The authors show that by actively driving the 89Y nuclear spins in the yttrium orthosilicate host crystal, the spin coherence time of the 153Eu3+ ions can be significantly extended.
AI.result: Driving the 89Y nuclear spins leads to a significant enhancement in the nuclear spin coherence time of 153Eu3+ ions in yttrium orthosilicate.
AI.conclusion: The improved spin coherence time achieved through driving host nuclear spins opens new avenues for enhancing the precision of measurements that utilize rare-earth-doped crystals.

title: Collective tunnel ionization in atomic systems
summary: We present a theory of the collective tunnel effect in atomic systems subject to strong low-frequency laser fields. Using an analytic semi-classical method and numerical solution to the time-dependent Schrodinger equation we demonstrate the collective channel of the nonsequential double ionization in neutral xenon and in the negative bromine ion. Collective tunneling in the presence of the electron-electron repulsion comprises the joint sub-barrier motion of the two electrons along quantum trajectories transversely shifted in opposite directions with respect to the direction of the external electric field. Momentum distributions of the electron pairs carry clear signatures of the collective channel in the form of shoulders in the direction lateral to the field polarization. We propose and discuss potential experimental approaches to a search for collective tunneling in atomic systems using short circularly polarized laser pulses.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a theory of collective tunneling in atomic systems under strong low-frequency laser fields, demonstrating a collective channel of nonsequential double ionization in xenon and negative bromine ions, where two electrons tunnel jointly through the sub-barrier region along trajectories transversely shifted in opposite directions relative to the field. Momentum distributions reveal signature shoulders lateral to field polarization, and experimental approaches using circularly polarized pulses are proposed.
AI.motivation: To develop a theoretical understanding of collective tunneling effects in strong-field ionization processes, specifically characterizing the joint sub-barrier motion of two electrons interacting in atomic systems under intense laser fields.
AI.method: Analytic semi-classical method combined with numerical solutions to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation; analysis of electron-pair momentum distributions.
AI.result: Identifies a collective tunneling channel in nonsequential double ionization of neutral xenon and negative bromine ions, where two electrons traverse the barrier jointly with transverse opposite shifts; collective channel manifes itself as shoulders in momentum distributions lateral to the field polarization.
AI.conclusion: Collective tunneling represents a distinct ionization mechanism detectable via characteristic momentum distribution signatures, and short circularly polarized laser pulses offer promising experimental routes for observing this effect.

title: Finite-Resolution Identifiability and Measurement Design for Molecular Conformer Spectroscopy
comment: 46 pages, 5 figures, and 5 tables. Includes 25 pages of supplementary material as an ancillary file. Reproducibility archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21712522
summary: Conformer assignment is meaningful only when the measurement can distinguish the candidate structures. We formulate conformer spectroscopy as a measurement-model-dependent identifiability problem in which each modality defines an observation law with explicit experimental and theoretical uncertainty. Equality of observation laws defines exact classes that refine as modalities are added, whereas finite-resolution ambiguity is non-transitive and is represented by a Bayes-error graph. We also give rank and constrained-Fisher criteria for population recovery from unnormalized additive spectra. The framework is applied to audited B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVP ensembles of 1,2-difluoroethane, ethylene glycol, and n-pentane. Under the declared shared-covariance working model, IR separates all non-mirror pairs, leaving only mirror pairs that are exactly degenerate under the achiral observation maps. This within-method result does not imply general IR sufficiency: in a six-case PBE0-to-B3LYP diagnostic, fixed calibration recovers one intended representative, whereas scale-and-shift profiling with a conservative cross-method covariance recovers five representatives and all six achiral classes. Under a combined stress-test covariance, n-pentane develops one non-mirror quotient ambiguity. Three individual Raman windows remove it, while no tested IR window does. Mirror-collapsed class populations remain identifiable and well conditioned under the calibrated-scale working model, whereas separate mirror-partner populations are exactly unidentifiable from achiral additive spectra.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates conformer spectroscopy as a measurement-model-dependent identifiability problem, where each modality defines an observation law with explicit uncertainties. Through rank and constrained-Fisher criteria, the framework is applied to audited DFT ensembles of 1,2-difluoroethane, ethylene glycol, and n-pentane. Results show IR separates all non-mirror pairs but leaves mirror degeneracies; Raman windows resolve some ambiguities; mirror-collapsed populations are identifiable while separate mirror-partner populations are exactly unidentifiable from achiral additive spectra.
AI.motivation: Conformer assignment is only meaningful when measurements can distinguish candidate structures, but existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for determining when and how well different spectroscopic modalities can resolve conformer populations given finite resolution and uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors formulate conformer spectroscopy as an identifiability problem where each modality defines an observation law with explicit experimental and theoretical uncertainty. Equality of observation laws defines exact classes refined by adding modalities; finite-resolution ambiguity is represented as a non-transitive Bayes-error graph. They derive rank and constrained-Fisher criteria for population recovery from unnormalized additive spectra, and apply the framework to B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVP ensembles under various covariance working models.
AI.result: Under a shared-covariance working model, IR separates all non-mirror conformer pairs. A PBE0-to-B3LYP six-case diagnostic shows fixed calibration recovers only one intended representative, while scale-and-shift profiling with conservative cross-method covariance recovers five representatives and all six achiral classes. Under a combined stress-test covariance, n-pentane develops one non-mirror quotient ambiguity; three Raman windows remove it while no tested IR window does. Mirror-collapsed populations remain identifiable and well conditioned, but separate mirror-partner populations are exactly unidentifiable from achiral additive spectra.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates measurement-model-dependent identifiability is essential for rigorous conformer assignment. While IR can separate non-mirror conformer classes under idealized covariances, its sufficiency does not generalize across methods. Raman windows provide supplementary resolving power for quotient ambiguities. Fundamental achiral observation maps make mirror-partner populations exactly unidentifiable, underscoring the need to collapse mirror classes for reliable population recovery.

title: Event-Based Spatial-Carrier Interferometry for Surface-Normal Vibration-Waveform Reconstruction
summary: Non-contact measurement of small vibrations perpendicular to a surface supports the evaluation of mechanical structures, but in camera-based interferometry, increasing the frame rate makes a trade-off with the field of view and spatial resolution. By recording only brightness changes, event cameras avoid this trade-off and reach high temporal and spatial resolution; our previously reported event topology-based visual vibrometer recovers vibration from apparent motion. This high-speed, high-resolution sensing is well suited to full-field measurement, yet such vibration produces too little apparent motion to capture its waveform. Here we show that event-based spatial-carrier interferometry reconstructs that waveform from moving interference fringes. That displacement moves the fringes, and signed event-density maps built from the event stream are demodulated at the spatial carrier to recover the interferometric phase and fix the otherwise ambiguous motion direction at turning points. Reconstructed waveforms agree with laser Doppler vibrometry over broad drive-frequency and amplitude ranges, with limits set by the maximum fringe speed and the sensor performance. Reconstruction is limited by a minimum aperture of about two fringe periods along the carrier and one along the fringes, which allows the surface to be mapped region by region. These results provide an empirical basis for full-field, spatially resolved interferometric vibrometry with event cameras as a non-contact measurement technique.

AI.tldr: This paper presents event-based spatial-carrier interferometry for non-contact vibration measurement. By leveraging event cameras that record only brightness changes, the technique circumvents the frame rate/field-of-view trade-off of conventional cameras. Vibration waveforms are reconstructed from moving interference fringes via demodulation of signed event-density maps at the spatial carrier, recovering interferometric phase and resolving motion direction at turning points. Results match laser Doppler vibrometry across broad frequency and amplitude ranges, with reconstruction limited by fringe speed and sensor performance, and requiring a minimum aperture of about two fringe periods along the carrier and one along the fringes.
AI.motivation: Camera-based interferometry for non-contact vibration measurement faces a fundamental trade-off between frame rate and field of view/spatial resolution. Event cameras avoid this by recording only brightness changes, but previous event-based visual vibrometry relied on apparent motion, which is insufficient for the tiny displacement created by such vibrations. The authors aim to use event-based spatial-carrier interferometry to recover full waveforms from interference fringes.
AI.method: The method uses event cameras to capture moving interference fringes produced by surface displacement. Signed event-density maps are built from the event stream and demodulated at the spatial carrier frequency to recover interferometric phase, fixing ambiguous motion direction at turning points. The technique measures small vibrations perpendicular to a surface by reconstructing the waveform from fringe motion, enabling full-field mapping by scanning regions with a minimum aperture of about two fringe periods along the carrier and one along the fringes.
AI.result: Reconstructed waveforms agree with laser Doppler vibrometry over broad drive-frequency and amplitude ranges. The main limits are the maximum fringe speed and sensor performance. Reconstruction requires a minimum aperture of roughly two fringe periods along the carrier direction and one along the fringes, which permits region-by-region surface mapping.
AI.conclusion: The results provide an empirical basis for full-field, spatially resolved interferometric vibrometry using event cameras as a non-contact measurement technique, overcoming the resolution and speed trade-offs inherent to frame-based interferometry.

title: A Spectral Route to Directed-Polymer Glasses
summary: A finite density of mutually avoiding directed polymers in a quenched random medium is a minimal model of glassy line matter. The dilute theory, solved by replica Bethe ansatz, predicts an interaction free energy proportional to $ρ^2$ and disorder cumulants with distinct power-law dependences on the density $ρ$, but direct numerical tests have been hindered by the combinatorially large many-polymer transfer matrix. We recast the problem as filling logarithmic eigenvalues of a single-polymer transfer-matrix product, obtaining the quenched free energy, its cumulants, and a disorder-induced linear spectral edge consistent with the replica prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a finite density of mutually avoiding directed polymers in a quenched random medium, a minimal model of glassy line matter. The authors recast the problem as filling logarithmic eigenvalues of a single-polymer transfer-matrix product, enabling numerical computation of the quenched free energy and its cumulants. Their results confirm the replica Bethe ansatz prediction of an interaction free energy proportional to ρ² and reveal a disorder-induced linear spectral edge consistent with the replica prediction.
AI.motivation: Direct numerical tests of the dilute theory of mutually avoiding directed polymers in random media—which predicts an interaction free energy proportional to ρ² and distinct power-law density dependences of disorder cumulants—have been hindered by the combinatorially large many-polymer transfer matrix. The authors aim to overcome this computational bottleneck.
AI.method: The problem is reformulated as filling logarithmic eigenvalues of a single-polymer transfer-matrix product. This approach allows the computation of the quenched free energy, its cumulants, and the spectral edge for finite densities of mutually avoiding directed polymers in a quenched random medium.
AI.result: The method yields the quenched free energy and its cumulants for finite polymer density, confirming the interaction free energy scales as ρ². A disorder-induced linear spectral edge is observed, consistent with the replica Bethe ansatz prediction.
AI.conclusion: The numerical results validate the dilute replica Bethe ansatz theory, confirming both the ρ² interaction free energy and the disorder-induced linear spectral edge, thereby providing a solid foundation for the minimal model of glassy line matter.

title: Resolving the Bubble Puzzle: Hydrogen Peroxide Formation Precedes Hydroxyl Radicals in Microbubbles and is Governed by Solid-Water Interfaces
summary: An alternative explanation is presented for recent reports that attribute sustained chemiluminescence (CL) and electrochemiluminescence (ECL) from electrogenerated microbubbles on steel or copper electrodes in aqueous luminol solutions (over 2-30 V range) to the spontaneous formation of hydroxyl radicals at the gas-water interface. Our experiments with a broad set of electrodes, viz., steel, copper, aluminium, and platinum, reveal that while microbubbles can be electrogenerated on all electrodes, CL is exhibited by steel and Cu only and not by Al and Pt. These observations establish that the gas-water interface of microbubbles is not the site for hydroxyl radical generation (else CL would be recorded in all cases). Complementary quantification of H2O2 in these experiments reveals its electrode dependence as follows: Al > Cu > Steel > Pt. This establishes that depending on the electrode, H2O2 forms first, and in some cases, hydroxyl radicals are observed (i.e., where CL/ECL is seen). Experiments with NMR and EPR spectroscopy revealed that: (i) H2O2 formation occurs only when O2 is present in water; and (ii) while steel and copper generate hydroxyl radicals through 1-electron reduction of H2O2, Al does not promote one-electron reduction of H2O2 to generate hydroxyl radicals, and Pt preferentially promotes disproportionation of H2O2 to H2O and O2. In fact, we demonstrate that H2O2 and hydroxyl radicals can be observed at specific metal-water interfaces even without microbubbles, confirming that the solid surface is the reactive site. Therefore, this work affords electrode-based predictions of whether or not electrogenerated microbubbles would yield CL in luminol solutions and calls into question the notion of spontaneous formation of hydroxyl radicals at gas-water interfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the claim that hydroxyl radicals spontaneously form at gas-water interfaces of electrogenerated microbubbles, demonstrating instead that the metal electrode surface is the reactive site. By testing multiple electrodes (steel, Cu, Al, Pt), the authors show that CL occurs only with steel and Cu, correlating with their ability to promote 1-electron reduction of H2O2 to hydroxyl radicals, whereas Al and Pt behave differently (no radical generation or H2O2 disproportionation).
AI.motivation: To provide an alternative, electrode-based explanation for sustained CL/ECL from electrogenerated microbubbles, and to critically evaluate the previously proposed mechanism involving spontaneous hydroxyl radical formation at gas-water interfaces.
AI.method: Experiments were conducted using a broad set of electrodes (steel, copper, aluminium, platinum) in aqueous luminol solutions over 2-30 V. CL observation, H2O2 quantification, NMR, and EPR spectroscopy were employed to probe radical formation and reaction pathways.
AI.result: Microbubbles were electrogenerated on all electrodes, but CL was only observed with steel and Cu. H2O2 quantification followed the order Al > Cu > Steel > Pt. NMR/EPR showed H2O2 forms only in the presence of O2; steel and Cu generate hydroxyl radicals via 1-electron reduction of H2O2, Al does not, and Pt promotes H2O2 disproportionation. H2O2 and hydroxyl radicals were observed at metal-water interfaces even without microbubbles.
AI.conclusion: The solid metal electrode surface—not the gas-water interface—is the reactive site for hydroxyl radical generation. The work enables electrode-based predictions of CL yield in luminol solutions and questions the concept of spontaneous radical formation at gas-water interfaces.

title: Pressure-induced Superconductivity in Thermoelectric Semiconductor Mg3Sb2
summary: The intrinsic electronic structures of narrow bandgap thermoelectric (TE) materials serve as a platform for the investigation of coupling effects of quasi-particles under high pressure, enabling the exploration of emerging electronic and phonon transport, superconductivity, and topological transition. Here, we report the discovery of pressure-induced superconductivity in the TE semiconductor Mg3Sb2. Upon the increased pressure, the metallization occurs at 8.7 GPa, followed by a superconducting transition concomitant with a carrier-type crossover from p- to n-type. This phenomenon arises from a pressure-induced structural phase transition from the semiconducting P-3m1 to the metallic C2/m-I phase. The superconducting critical temperature (Tc) exhibits a dome-shaped pressure dependence, peaking at 3.3 K at 12.6 GPa. Combined theoretical calculations, high-pressure Raman spectroscopy, and X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements reveal an additional structural transition above 20 GPa, yielding a distinct C2/m-II phase. Our findings establish the high-pressure phase diagram of Mg3Sb2, elucidate its pressure-dependent electronic properties, and provide valuable insights for future investigations of TE materials under high pressure.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of pressure-induced superconductivity in the thermoelectric semiconductor Mg3Sb2. Metallization occurs at 8.7 GPa with a structural phase transition from semiconducting P-3m1 to metallic C2/m-I, accompanied by a p- to n-type carrier crossover. The superconducting critical temperature shows a dome-shaped pressure dependence peaking at 3.3 K at 12.6 GPa, and a second structural transition to C2/m-II occurs above 20 GPa, establishing the high-pressure phase diagram of Mg3Sb2.
AI.motivation: To investigate the intrinsic electronic structures of narrow bandgap thermoelectric materials under high pressure, which serve as a platform for exploring coupling effects of quasi-particles, enabling the discovery of emergent electronic and phonon transport, superconductivity, and topological transitions.
AI.method: Combined experimental and theoretical approach including high-pressure electrical transport measurements, high-pressure Raman spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and theoretical calculations to track structural and electronic phase transitions in Mg3Sb2.
AI.result: Metallization occurs at 8.7 GPa followed by a superconducting transition with a p- to n-type carrier crossover, arising from a structural transition from P-3m1 to C2/m-I. Tc exhibits a dome-shaped pressure dependence peaking at 3.3 K at 12.6 GPa. An additional structural transition to C2/m-II is identified above 20 GPa.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish the high-pressure phase diagram of Mg3Sb2, elucidate its pressure-dependent electronic properties, and provide valuable insights for future investigations of thermoelectric materials under high pressure.

title: 1+1d Lattice Dirac Fermions from Non-Onsite Vector and Axial Symmetries
summary: We construct an exactly solvable Hamiltonian lattice model realizing a 1+1d Dirac fermion, with exact microscopic vector and axial vector $U(1)$ symmetries. The mixed anomaly between these is accommodated by the not-on-site action of the symmetries. Our Hilbert space is a $Z_2$-graded tensor product of local $Z_2$-graded Hilbert spaces which include infinite dimensional rotor degrees of freedom. The Hamiltonian becomes manifestly exactly solvable after a locality-preserving unitary mapping to an equivalent fermionic Villain Hilbert space. Our construction also allows an exactly solvable realization of interacting fermionic Luttinger liquids. At the free Dirac fixed point, our Hamiltonian contains irrelevant interactions, which we compute to leading order.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs an exactly solvable Hamiltonian lattice model for a 1+1d Dirac fermion with exact microscopic vector and axial U(1) symmetries. The mixed anomaly between these symmetries is realized through not-on-site symmetry actions. The Hilbert space is a Z2-graded tensor product including infinite-dimensional rotor degrees of freedom. A locality-preserving unitary maps the model to an equivalent fermionic Villain Hilbert space, making the Hamiltonian exactly solvable. The construction extends to interacting fermionic Luttinger liquids, and at the free Dirac fixed point, irrelevant interactions are computed to leading order.
AI.motivation: The goal is to find a lattice regularization that preserves the chiral (axial) symmetry exactly while accommodating the mixed vector/axial anomaly, which is notoriously difficult on the lattice. The authors aim to construct an exactly solvable model that realizes a 1+1d Dirac fermion with exact microscopic symmetries and their anomalies.
AI.method: The model uses a Z2-graded tensor product of local Z2-graded Hilbert spaces that include infinite-dimensional rotor degrees of freedom. The symmetries act not on-site, which accommodates the mixed anomaly. A locality-preserving unitary transformation maps the system to a fermionic Villain Hilbert space where the Hamiltonian becomes exactly solvable. The approach is generalized to interacting Luttinger liquids.
AI.result: An exactly solvable Hamiltonian lattice model realizing a 1+1d Dirac fermion with exact vector and axial U(1) symmetries is constructed. The mixed anomaly is handled by non-on-site symmetry actions. The construction works for both free Dirac fermions (with computable irrelevant interactions at the fixed point) and interacting fermionic Luttinger liquids.
AI.conclusion: The construction provides a rigorous lattice framework that preserves exact chiral symmetry and realizes the mixed anomaly, avoiding the need for on-site symmetry realizations. It offers an exactly solvable handle on Dirac fermions and Luttinger liquids on the lattice.

title: Computing with traceable tensor networks
summary: We introduce a new SVD-based tensor decomposition method for tensor networks with arbitrary graph topologies, extending classical hierarchical SVD-based techniques to networks with cycles and general connectivity. We also introduce addition and rounding procedures for traceable tensor graphs, enabling step-rounding time integration of high-dimensional PDEs directly in graph format, with rank truncation controlled to a prescribed tolerance at every time step. We demonstrate the new method on the decomposition of multivariate functions and on the numerical solution of the Fokker-Planck equation, and find that the graph-format representation attains comparable or better accuracy than the classical tensor train and hierarchical Tucker tensor formats, while using substantially fewer degrees of freedom at lower computational cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a novel SVD-based tensor decomposition method for tensor networks with arbitrary graph topologies (including cycles and general connectivity), along with addition and rounding procedures for traceable tensor graphs. This enables step-rounding time integration of high-dimensional PDEs directly in graph format, demonstrated on multivariate function decomposition and the Fokker-Planck equation, achieving comparable or better accuracy than tensor train and hierarchical Tucker formats with fewer degrees of freedom and lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Classical hierarchical SVD-based tensor decomposition techniques are limited to specific topologies (e.g., tensor trains and hierarchical Tucker formats), and cannot handle tensor networks with cycles or general connectivity. There is a need for a decomposition method that works on arbitrary graph topologies to enable more flexible and efficient representations of high-dimensional data and efficient time integration of high-dimensional PDEs.
AI.method: The authors develop a new SVD-based tensor decomposition method applicable to tensor networks with arbitrary graph topologies, extending classical hierarchical SVD approaches to handle cycles and general connectivity. They also devise addition and rounding procedures for traceable tensor graphs, which permit step-rounding time integration of high-dimensional PDEs directly in graph format, with rank truncation controlled to a prescribed tolerance at every time step.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on multivariate function decomposition and numerical solution of the Fokker-Planck equation. The graph-format representation achieves comparable or better accuracy than classical tensor train and hierarchical Tucker tensor formats, while using substantially fewer degrees of freedom at lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The graph-based tensor decomposition approach is a viable and efficient alternative to classical tensor formats, offering greater topological flexibility, improved accuracy, and reduced computational and memory requirements for high-dimensional problems.

title: Universal crossovers in weakly-monitored quantum critical states
summary: We study post-measurement ensembles of ground states of tricritical and critical 1D quantum Ising Hamiltonians subjected, respectively, to weak energy and spin measurements without post-selection. These measurements act as relevant perturbations about the unmeasured critical ground states. Using finite-size renormalization group (RG) crossover analyses, we characterize their universal properties through the entanglement effective central charge, effective Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy, and signatures of multifractality from moments of measurement-averaged correlation functions. In both cases, we find evidence for "measurement-dominated" or "measurement-altered" fixed points governed by the underlying Born-rule randomness. For critical Ising, we find a direct RG flow to a projective-measurement fixed point with area-law entanglement, whereas for the tricritical Ising model, we find evidence for a weak-measurement fixed point with logarithmic entanglement. These results clarify the RG-flow structure of weakly measured multicritical Ising ground states and show how intrinsic measurement-induced randomness can generate complex and rich universal long-distance scaling behavior in the post-measurement ensembles, accessible to controlled analytical RG and numerical finite-size RG crossover analyses.

AI.tldr: This paper studies post-measurement ensembles of 1D quantum Ising ground states under weak energy and spin measurements without post-selection, using finite-size RG crossover analyses. They find that measurements act as relevant perturbations about critical ground states, leading to measurement-dominated/measurement-altered fixed points governed by Born-rule randomness. For critical Ising, a projective-measurement fixed point with area-law entanglement emerges; for tricritical Ising, a weak-measurement fixed point with logarithmic entanglement is found.
AI.motivation: To understand how weak measurements (without post-selection) act as relevant perturbations on critical/multicritical 1D quantum Ising ground states, and to characterize the universal properties of the resulting post-measurement ensembles, particularly the RG-flow structure and measurement-induced randomness effects.
AI.method: Finite-size renormalization group (RG) crossover analyses applied to post-measurement ensembles of ground states of tricritical and critical 1D quantum Ising Hamiltonians. Characterization is performed via the entanglement effective central charge, effective Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy, and moments of measurement-averaged correlation functions (for multifractality signatures).
AI.result: Evidence is found for measurement-dominated (critical Ising) and measurement-altered (tricritical Ising) fixed points governed by Born-rule randomness. Critical Ising flows directly to a projective-measurement fixed point with area-law entanglement, while tricritical Ising exhibits a weak-measurement fixed point with logarithmic entanglement.
AI.conclusion: Weakly measured multicritical Ising ground states exhibit rich universal long-distance scaling behavior in post-measurement ensembles, driven by intrinsic measurement-induced randomness. The findings clarify the RG-flow structure of such systems and demonstrate that the behavior is accessible via controlled analytical RG and numerical finite-size RG crossover analyses.

title: Nonlocality-induced critical-length hierarchy from non-Hermitian competition
summary: Spectral transitions in non-Hermitian lattices often arise from the competition between non-reciprocal skin accumulation and inter-component hybridization. In short-range systems formed by two coupled chains, this competition conventionally leads to the logarithmic critical-length law $N_c\sim\ln D$, where $D$ is the transverse separation between the chains. Here we show that long-range hoppings fundamentally reorganizes this critical behavior, producing a hierarchy of distinct scaling laws. When only the hybridization couplings are power-law decaying with exponent $α$, the onset becomes algebraic, $N_c\sim D^{α/3}$. When the hoppings within each chain are themselves also power-law decaying, in addition to the hybridization couplings, the system enters a scale-covariant regime for $α<2$, in which the criticality threshold equation depends only on the system aspect ratio $N_c/D$. At $α=2$ and beyond, this regime is followed by a marginal logarithmically corrected and algebraically corrected regimes, respectively. We identify two new non-local mechanisms that enable this unconventional critical hierarchy: a nonanalytic band-edge dispersion from long-range intra-chain hoppings, and parity-mixing hybridization induced by non-reciprocity. Our results show that nonlocality systematically removes the physical length scales i.e. skin depth underlying conventional critical non-Hermitian skin behavior, offering a platform-independent framework testable in programmable topoelectrical circuits, photonic lattices and digital quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that long-range hoppings fundamentally alter the critical-length scaling in non-Hermitian coupled-chain lattices, producing a hierarchy of scaling laws (algebraic N_c~D^{α/3}, scale-covariant regime for α<2, and marginal logarithmic/algebraic corrections at α=2 and beyond) instead of the conventional logarithmic law N_c~ln D found in short-range systems.
AI.motivation: To understand how nonlocality (long-range hoppings) reorganizes the conventional critical behavior of non-Hermitian topological systems, where short-range coupled chains exhibit a logarithmic critical-length law N_c~ln D that defines the skin depth scale.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze two coupled non-Hermitian chains with long-range hoppings. They consider two cases: (1) only hybridization couplings decay as a power law with exponent α, and (2) both intra-chain and hybridization hoppings are power-law decaying. They derive the criticality threshold equations and identify the scaling laws via the onset of non-reciprocal skin accumulation against inter-component hybridization.
AI.result: The paper finds a hierarchy of critical scaling laws: algebraic onset N_c~D^{α/3} when only hybridization is long-range; a scale-covariant regime depending only on the aspect ratio N_c/D for α<2 when both intra-chain and hybridization hoppings are long-range; and logarithmically/algebraically corrected regimes at α=2 and beyond. Two new non-local mechanisms are identified: nonanalytic band-edge dispersion from long-range intra-chain hopping and parity-mixing hybridization from non-reciprocity.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocality systematically removes physical length scales (such as the skin depth) underlying conventional critical non-Hermitian skin behavior, offering a platform-independent framework testable in programmable topoelectrical circuits, photonic lattices, and digital quantum simulators.

title: Investigation of GeSn aspect ratio trapping growth up to 8% Sn
summary: Aspect ratio trapping (ART) growth of germanium-tin (GeSn) is a promising approach to target important objectives on the quest towards commercialization of complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible GeSn optoelectronics devices. Its local growth on patterned substrate allows for versatile device integration into photonics integrated circuit or for stand-alone structure like focal plane array imager. Additionally, high aspect ratio from nano-sized window can terminate early threading dislocation propagation on the oxide sidewalls, leaving subsequent growth defect-free and potentially improving the device performance. Knowledge remains missing regarding GeSn ART growth kinetics, morphology and how they evolve from thin film growth, with successful growth itself yet to be demonstrated. In this work, we report GeSn ART growth up to 8% Sn. Two configurations -- self-induced Ge core/GeSn shell for Sn content between 6% and 8%, and bulk GeSn ART for Sn content below 1% -- are observed. We present a comprehensive study on GeSn ART growth kinetics through different growth rounds and designs, showing a link between pyramid shape of ART island and successful Sn incorporation, as well as the role of growth selectivity and local heating.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first demonstration of germanium-tin (GeSn) aspect ratio trapping (ART) growth with Sn content up to 8%, identifying two growth configurations (Ge core/GeSn shell and bulk GeSn ART) and providing a comprehensive study of growth kinetics, morphology, and the factors influencing successful Sn incorporation.
AI.motivation: GeSn ART growth is a promising route toward CMOS-compatible GeSn optoelectronics, offering versatile device integration and defect termination via high aspect ratio nano-sized windows. However, knowledge of GeSn ART growth kinetics and morphology remains missing, and successful growth had not yet been demonstrated.
AI.method: Report GeSn ART growth up to 8% Sn, studying growth kinetics through different growth rounds and designs. Two configurations are observed: self-induced Ge core/GeSn shell for Sn content between 6-8%, and bulk GeSn ART for Sn content below 1%. The study links pyramid-shaped ART islands to successful Sn incorporation and examines the roles of growth selectivity and local heating.
AI.result: GeSn ART growth was successfully demonstrated with Sn content up to 8%. Two distinct growth configurations were identified depending on Sn concentration range. A correlation between the pyramid shape of ART islands and successful Sn incorporation was established, along with insights into growth selectivity and local heating effects.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first comprehensive understanding of GeSn ART growth kinetics and morphology, demonstrating successful GeSn ART growth up to 8% Sn and paving the way toward CMOS-compatible GeSn optoelectronics and photonic integrated circuit integration.

title: Thermodynamically consistent initialization of the Maxwell--Cattaneo---Vernotte heat conduction model: Analytical solutions and engineering applications
summary: This paper investigates the numerical initialization of the one-dimensional Maxwell--Cattaneo--Vernotte (MCV) heat conduction model, addressing the critical mathematical challenge of defining the initial time derivative for non-equilibrium states. In modern high-frequency thermal engineering applications, traditional time-integration schemes and commercial finite-element solvers frequently introduce severe numerical artifacts when handling non-Fourier models. This study systematically evaluates three initialization strategies: a zero derivative, a spatially uniform non-zero derivative, and an exact space-dependent derivative. Using an explicit staggered finite-difference scheme, the transient responses to an exponentially distributed initial temperature field under adiabatic boundary conditions are compared against an analytical solution using the Galerkin method. The results demonstrate that assuming a zero or spatially uniform initial derivative introduces significant unphysical oscillatory deviations, leading to heat-flux prediction errors as the relaxation time increases. Conversely, mapping the exact space-dependent derivative onto the staggered grid preserves the local thermodynamic structure of the initial state, yielding robust transient responses that match the analytical benchmark without meaningful computational overhead. These findings establish a thermodynamically consistent initialization technique that can be extended to non-local models as well.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the numerical initialization of the one-dimensional Maxwell-Cattaneo-Vernotte (MCV) heat conduction model, focusing on defining the initial time derivative for non-equilibrium states. Three initialization strategies—zero derivative, spatially uniform derivative, and exact space-dependent derivative—are evaluated using an explicit staggered finite-difference scheme against a Galerkin analytical solution. Results show that zero or uniform initial derivatives produce unphysical oscillations and heat-flux errors, while the exact space-dependent derivative preserves thermodynamic consistency and matches the analytical benchmark without computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Traditional time-integration schemes and commercial finite-element solvers introduce severe numerical artifacts when handling non-Fourier (MCV) models in high-frequency thermal engineering. A critical mathematical challenge exists in defining the initial time derivative for non-equilibrium states, which has not been systematically addressed.
AI.method: Three initialization strategies (zero, spatially uniform non-zero, and exact space-dependent initial derivative) are compared. An explicit staggered finite-difference scheme simulates transient responses to an exponentially distributed initial temperature field under adiabatic boundary conditions, benchmarked against a Galerkin analytical solution.
AI.result: Zero or uniform initial derivatives cause significant unphysical oscillatory deviations and heat-flux prediction errors that grow with relaxation time. The exact space-dependent derivative mapped onto the staggered grid preserves the local thermodynamic structure, producing robust transient responses matching the analytical benchmark without meaningful computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a thermodynamically consistent initialization technique for non-Fourier heat conduction that ensures accurate transient predictions, and the approach is extendable to non-local models.

title: Analytical results of Typical Medium Theory for the Bethe lattice with Cauchy disorder
summary: We present a combined numerical and analytically tractable realization of the typical medium theory (TMT) for Anderson localization on the infinite-connectivity Bethe lattice with Cauchy-distributed on-site disorder. Exploiting the special properties of the Cauchy distribution and the Bethe lattice, we derive an analytical expression for the typical density of states (TDOS) and obtain a simplified TMT self-consistency scheme. We show that the TDOS at the band center decreases linearly with disorder strength and vanishes at the critical disorder $W_c=D/2$. The resulting $ω$--$W$ phase diagram reveals the continuous collapse of the mobility edge and the disappearance of extended states.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analytically tractable realization of typical medium theory (TMT) for Anderson localization on an infinite-connectivity Bethe lattice with Cauchy-distributed disorder, deriving an analytical expression for the typical density of states (TDOS) and showing that TDOS vanishes at critical disorder Wc=D/2, with a phase diagram revealing continuous collapse of the mobility edge.
AI.motivation: To provide a combined numerical and analytical treatment of Anderson localization on the Bethe lattice that goes beyond purely numerical approaches, leveraging the special properties of Cauchy distribution to obtain closed-form analytical results for the typical medium theory.
AI.method: Combines the typical medium theory (TMT) framework with the infinite-connectivity Bethe lattice and Cauchy-distributed on-site disorder. By exploiting the special properties of the Cauchy distribution and Bethe lattice structure, an analytical expression for the typical density of states (TDOS) is derived, leading to a simplified TMT self-consistency scheme.
AI.result: The TDOS at the band center decreases linearly with disorder strength and vanishes at the critical disorder Wc=D/2. The resulting ω-W phase diagram shows the continuous collapse of the mobility edge and the disappearance of extended states.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rare analytically tractable realization of TMT for Anderson localization, establishing a clear quantitative picture of localization on the Bethe lattice and identifying the critical disorder threshold where all extended states vanish.

title: Pressure induced magnetic-field-free superconducting diode effect in NbSe2 flake
summary: The superconducting diode effect (SDE) is a fascinating nonreciprocal phenomenon where the critical current is different for opposite current directions. It is widely believed that realizing SDE requires breaking both inversion symmetry (IS) and time-reversal symmetry (TRS), which are usually achieved via heterostructure engineering and applying external magnetic fields. Here, we report a pressure-induced magnetic-field-free SDE in NbSe2 flakes without any heterostructures. We show that pressure alone breaks the IS, as confirmed by the second harmonic generation. Crucially, upon applying an out-of-plane magnetic field (B), the SDE exhibits even-in-B behavior, implying the absence of explicit TRS breaking. This finding challenges the prevailing theoretical paradigm and demonstrates that a magnetic-field-free SDE can emerge without explicitly breaking TRS. Thereby, our work establishes pressure engineering as a powerful tool for inducing nonreciprocal superconductivity and designing versatile, magnetic-field-free superconducting devices.

AI.tldr: Pressure alone can induce a magnetic-field-free superconducting diode effect (SDE) in NbSe2 flakes without heterostructures, where the SDE shows even-in-B behavior, indicating that explicit time-reversal symmetry breaking is not required.
AI.motivation: The conventional paradigm holds that realizing the superconducting diode effect requires breaking both inversion symmetry and time-reversal symmetry, typically through heterostructure engineering and external magnetic fields. The authors aim to challenge this paradigm and explore whether a magnetic-field-free SDE can be achieved without explicit TRS breaking.
AI.method: The authors apply pressure to NbSe2 flakes to break inversion symmetry, confirmed via second harmonic generation measurements. They then characterize the SDE and examine its dependence on an out-of-plane magnetic field, observing even-in-B behavior.
AI.result: Pressure alone breaks inversion symmetry and induces a magnetic-field-free SDE in NbSe2. The SDE exhibits even-in-B magnetic field dependence, indicating the absence of explicit time-reversal symmetry breaking, which contradicts the prevailing theoretical framework.
AI.conclusion: Pressure engineering is established as a powerful tool for inducing nonreciprocal superconductivity and designing versatile, magnetic-field-free superconducting devices, demonstrating that magnetic-field-free SDE can emerge without explicitly breaking TRS.

title: Spin-charge separation in the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model
summary: Recent experiments in moiré materials have enabled the realization of a variety of exotic quantum phases. In this context, the Hofstadter-Hubbard model has been proposed as a possible setting for hosting chiral spin liquid. Concurrently, significant progress has been recently made in the computational methods for two-dimensional many-body fermion systems, which makes numerically studying this challenging model a real possibility in genuine 2D geometry. Motivated by these advances, we investigate the putative chiral spin liquid phase in the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model using variational Monte Carlo with neural quantum states (NQS) and projected entangled pair states (PEPS). We observe spin-charge separation directly in real space through numerical spin-pumping simulation and real-time spin and charge motion. In addition, in the context of anyonic superconductivity conjectured in this model, we find a positive two-electron binding energy on small systems, but it decreases below our numerical resolution as the system size increases. Our work demonstrates NQS and PEPS as powerful tools, capable of cross-checking each other, for diagnosing topological order and fractionalized excitations in strongly correlated electronic systems.

AI.tldr: The authors use variational Monte Carlo with neural quantum states (NQS) and projected entangled pair states (PEPS) to investigate the putative chiral spin liquid phase in the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model, observing spin-charge separation directly in real space and finding that conjectured anyonic superconductivity's two-electron binding energy vanishes with increasing system size.
AI.motivation: Moiré materials enable exotic quantum phases, and the Hofstadter-Hubbard model has been proposed as a candidate for hosting chiral spin liquids. Recent advances in computational methods for 2D many-body fermion systems make it feasible to numerically study this challenging model in genuine 2D geometry.
AI.method: The authors employ variational Monte Carlo with neural quantum states (NQS) and projected entangled pair states (PEPS) to study the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model, performing real-space numerical spin-pumping simulations and real-time spin and charge motion tracking to diagnose fractionalized excitations.
AI.result: Direct real-space evidence of spin-charge separation is observed. For anyonic superconductivity, a positive two-electron binding energy is found on small systems, but it falls below numerical resolution as system size increases. The two methods cross-validate each other in diagnosing topological order.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that NQS and PEPS are powerful, mutually cross-checking computational tools for diagnosing topological order and fractionalized excitations in strongly correlated electronic systems.

title: A Unified Graph Neural Network Framework for Non-Equilibrium Carrier and Lattice Dynamics Driven by Electric Fields
summary: Finite-temperature simulations of electric-field-driven dynamics need a unified description of interatomic interactions, local electronic states, and configuration-dependent electric responses. First-principles simulations remain scale-limited, whereas conventional machine-learning potentials lack electric-field effects. Recent machine-learning frameworks have incorporated electric-field response or atom-resolved electronic-state information, but rarely both within a single framework. Here, we develop an electric-field-response graph neural network (EFR-GNN) that predicts energies, forces, Born effective charge tensors, atom-resolved charges and magnetic moments, and supports long-time field-driven molecular dynamics with atom-resolved tracking of localized electronic states. In hole-doped MgO, static fields rectify thermally activated hole-polaron hopping through a forward--backward asymmetry quantified by a nearest-neighbor model. In GaAs, resonant terahertz excitation generates a coherent $Γ$-point transverse-optical phonon with dephasing consistent with experiment, while opposite helicities reverse its rotation. In superionic $α$-AgI, it reproduces temperature-dependent Ag$^+$ mobility and collective field-driven ionic drift. Together, EFR-GNN offers an approach to finite-temperature simulations of field-driven atomic and localized-carrier dynamics.

AI.tldr: EFR-GNN is a graph neural network that unifies electric-field-response predictions (energies, forces, Born effective charge tensors, atom-resolved charges, magnetic moments) with long-time field-driven molecular dynamics, enabling finite-temperature simulations of field-driven atomic and localized-carrier dynamics across diverse materials.
AI.motivation: Finite-temperature simulations of electric-field-driven dynamics require simultaneous description of interatomic interactions, local electronic states, and configuration-dependent electric responses. First-principles methods are scale-limited, and conventional machine-learning potentials lack electric-field effects. Existing ML frameworks typically incorporate either electric-field response or electronic-state information, but rarely both.
AI.method: The authors develop an electric-field-response graph neural network (EFR-GNN) that predicts energies, forces, Born effective charge tensors, atom-resolved charges, and magnetic moments while supporting long-time field-driven molecular dynamics with atom-resolved tracking of localized electronic states.
AI.result: In hole-doped MgO, static fields rectify thermally activated hole-polaron hopping with forward-backward asymmetry quantified by a nearest-neighbor model. In GaAs, resonant THz excitation generates coherent Γ-point transverse-optical phonons with dephasing matching experiment, and opposite helicities reverse rotation. In superionic α-AgI, the model reproduces temperature-dependent Ag+ mobility and collective field-driven ionic drift.
AI.conclusion: EFR-GNN provides a unified approach to finite-temperature simulations of field-driven atomic and localized-carrier dynamics, bridging the gap between electric-field responses and local electronic states in a single ML framework.

title: Fractal deconfinement and confinement in Sierpinski ice
summary: We study the six-vertex model on the Sierpinski gasket, a four-coordinated hierarchical fractal with Hausdorff dimension $d_f=\log_23$. Given the importance of dimensionality for the long-wavelength behavior of such models, we specifically consider correlations and confinement as a function of the vertex weights, with the equal-weight point corresponding to the ice model. We calculate the partition function and correlators recursively to obtain a rich phase diagram hosting many different regimes. While the ice model shows entropic charge confinement, a particular four-vertex limit exhibits fractal deconfinement, with the string joining the deconfined charges itself a statistical fractal with fractal dimension $d_l=\log_2(5/2)\approx 1.3$. Finally, we propose a setup as an artificial spin ice to enable experimental study of the rich phenomenology of Sierpinski ice and its generalisations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the six-vertex model on a Sierpinski gasket (a hierarchical fractal) and derives its phase diagram via recursive computation of partition functions and correlators. It finds entropic charge confinement in the ice model but fractal deconfinement in a four-vertex limit, where the string connecting deconfined charges is itself a statistical fractal. A physical realization as artificial spin ice is proposed.
AI.motivation: To understand how the fractal dimensionality of the Sierpinski gasket (df = log2 3) affects the long-wavelength behavior of vertex models, particularly correlations and charge confinement, which are dimensionality-sensitive properties.
AI.method: Recursive computation of the partition function and correlation functions on the Sierpinski gasket as a function of vertex weights, exploiting the hierarchical self-similar structure of the fractal lattice. A four-vertex limit is identified for the deconfinement regime, and an artificial spin ice setup is proposed for experimental realization.
AI.result: A rich phase diagram with many regimes is obtained. The ice model shows entropic charge confinement, while a special four-vertex limit displays fractal deconfinement where the charge-connecting string becomes a statistical fractal with fractal dimension dl = log2(5/2) ≈ 1.3.
AI.conclusion: Fractal geometry fundamentally alters the physics of the six-vertex model, leading to novel phases including fractal deconfinement not observed in regular lattices, and this phenomenology can be accessed experimentally via artificial spin ice designs.

title: Broken site symmetry of Fe adatoms on Bi$_2$Te$_3$
summary: We report a combined scanning tunneling microscopy and atomistic theoretical study of Fe adatoms on the Bi$_2$Te$_3$(111) surface. Topographic imaging at $4.5$~K shows Fe adatoms in fcc and hcp hollow sites exhibit a threefold-symmetric contrast, consistent with the $C_{3v}$ symmetry of the adsorption site. However, simultaneously acquired differential conductance ($dI/dV$) maps reveal a pronounced reduction in symmetry, evidenced by differential contrast observed at nearest-neighbor Te sites. Density functional theory calculations show that the Fe/Bi$_2$Te$_3$ system undergoes a static Jahn--Teller distortion, reducing the adsorption symmetry from $C_{3v}$ to $C_{1v}$, with the distorted configuration favored by $72.5$~meV. Orbital-projected density of states calculations show that the occupied states near the Fermi level are dominated by $d_{xz}$ and $d_{yz}$ orbitals, whereas the unoccupied states are primarily of $d_{z^2}$, $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{xy}$ character. The local density of states from these orbitals is in good qualitative agreement with experimental $dI/dV$ spectra. Furthermore, simulated local-density-of-states maps using a tight-binding Green's function approach are in good agreement with experimental $dI/dV$ maps, confirming that the reduced symmetry originates from the $C_{1v}$ structural distortion.

AI.tldr: A combined STM and DFT study reveals that Fe adatoms on Bi₂Te₃(111) undergo a static Jahn-Teller distortion, reducing the adsorption symmetry from C₃v to C₁v. This distortion, favored by 72.5 meV, explains the reduced symmetry observed in differential conductance maps, with orbital-projected DOS and simulated LDOS maps confirming the origin of the symmetry reduction.
AI.motivation: To understand the symmetry reduction observed in dI/dV maps of Fe adatoms on Bi₂Te₃(111) compared to their topographic imaging, and to identify the underlying electronic and structural mechanism.
AI.method: Combined scanning tunneling microscopy (topographic imaging and dI/dV mapping at 4.5 K) with density functional theory calculations, including orbital-projected density of states analysis and tight-binding Green's function simulations of local density of states maps.
AI.result: Fe adatoms in fcc and hcp hollow sites show threefold-symmetric topography but reduced differential contrast symmetry via a Jahn-Teller distortion from C₃v to C₁v, favored by 72.5 meV. Occupied states near E_F are dominated by d_xz and d_yz orbitals, while unoccupied states are d_z², d_x²−y², and d_xy. Simulated LDOS maps match experimental dI/dV maps, confirming the C₁v distortion.
AI.conclusion: The experimentally observed symmetry reduction in dI/dV maps of Fe on Bi₂Te₃(111) is caused by a static Jahn-Teller distortion that lowers the adsorption site symmetry from C₃v to C₁v, with theoretical simulations corroborating this interpretation.

title: Physics-Informed and Knowledge-Driven Generative AI for Autonomous Discovery of Porous Oxide Energy Materials: Opportunities and Challenges
summary: The discovery of next-generation energy-storage materials is increasingly limited by the complexity of the underlying design problem rather than by computational capability alone. Porous transition-metal oxides represent a particularly challenging class of battery materials because their performance emerges from coupled interactions among crystal chemistry, pore architecture, ion transport, electrochemistry, electro-chemo-mechanics, synthesis, manufacturing, and battery-system operation. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities for generating chemically plausible crystal structures. However, current approaches remain largely focused on crystallographic validity and thermodynamic stability. This perspective presents a roadmap for advancing generative AI beyond crystal generation toward physics-informed, application-aware, and synthesis-aware inverse design. Using porous oxide electrodes as a representative materials platform, we propose a seven-tier physics-informed inverse-design framework integrating chemistry, thermodynamics, transport, electrochemistry, durability, cell compatibility, and manufacturability. We further identify the "Missing Data Problem" as a fundamental bottleneck limiting application-aware AI and introduce an autonomous knowledge-generation framework supported by a Porous Oxide Energy Materials Ontology and a continuously evolving "Knowledge Base". Together, these concepts establish the foundation for Synthesis-Aware, Closed-Loop Autonomous Discovery, providing a general framework for AI-enabled autonomous materials discovery across energy-storage materials and other functional materials.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper proposes a roadmap for advancing generative AI in materials discovery beyond mere crystal structure generation toward physics-informed, application-aware, and synthesis-aware inverse design, using porous transition-metal oxide battery electrodes as the representative platform. It introduces a seven-tier inverse-design framework and addresses the "Missing Data Problem" through an autonomous knowledge-generation framework built on an ontology and evolving knowledge base to enable closed-loop autonomous materials discovery.
AI.motivation: The discovery of next-generation energy-storage materials is increasingly bottlenecked by design complexity rather than computational power. While generative AI can produce chemically plausible crystal structures, current approaches focus narrowly on crystallographic validity and thermodynamic stability, ignoring the coupled multi-scale interactions—crystal chemistry, pore architecture, ion transport, electrochemistry, electro-chemo-mechanics, synthesis, manufacturing, and system-level operation—that determine real battery performance.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a seven-tier physics-informed inverse-design framework integrating chemistry, thermodynamics, transport, electrochemistry, durability, cell compatibility, and manufacturability; (2) identify the "Missing Data Problem" as a fundamental bottleneck; (3) introduce an autonomous knowledge-generation framework supported by a Porous Oxide Energy Materials Ontology and a continuously evolving Knowledge Base to enable Synthesis-Aware, Closed-Loop Autonomous Discovery.
AI.result: The paper delivers a conceptual roadmap and framework architecture rather than empirical results, establishing the foundations for physics-informed, application-aware, and synthesis-aware generative AI inverse design for porous oxide electrodes, and proposing infrastructure (ontology + knowledge base) to overcome data scarcity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Synthesis-Aware, Closed-Loop Autonomous Discovery framework provides a general paradigm extendable beyond porous oxides to other energy-storage and functional materials, arguing that generation must be guided by full application context and continuously evolving knowledge to achieve practical AI-enabled autonomous materials discovery.

title: Circuit-Level Design, Modeling, and On-Wafer Characterization of a Coplanar THz Optoelectronic Mixer
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Terahertz Science and Technology. 11 pages, 11 figures
summary:
We report the design, modeling, and on-wafer characterization of a photoconductive heterodyne mixer implemented as a true terahertz monolithic integrated circuit (TMIC). Unlike previous photoconductive heterodyne demonstrations, the proposed circuit is characterized using RF integrated circuit metrics including input return loss, RF/IF isolation, broadband impedance matching, and conversion loss.
  The mixer combines a microcavity photoconductor with a broadband coplanar matching network incorporating a Ti shunt resistor, an RF DC-blocking MIM capacitor, and an RF/IF decoupling capacitor. A circuit-level model including both the photoconductor and the distributed CPW accesses is developed and validated.
  The passive circuit is experimentally characterized up to 500 GHz using on-wafer VNA measurements and accurately reproduced by simulation. Under illumination, the model predicts an input reflection coefficient below -10 dB up to 215 GHz and better than -6.5 dB up to 500 GHz. Measured and simulated conversion losses agree within +/-1 dB over the entire 1-500 GHz range. Conversion loss varies from 22.5-25.5 dB below 320 GHz and 26-34 dB up to 500 GHz. The proposed TMIC demonstrates broadband operation and provides a validated circuit design methodology for future integrated THz photonic mixers.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the design, modeling, and on-wafer characterization of a photoconductive heterodyne mixer implemented as a true terahertz monolithic integrated circuit (TMIC), characterized using RF integrated circuit metrics. The mixer integrates a microcavity photoconductor with a broadband coplanar matching network. The passive circuit is validated up to 500 GHz via on-wafer VNA measurements, with simulated conversion losses agreeing within ±1 dB over the 1-500 GHz range (22.5-25.5 dB below 320 GHz; 26-34 dB up to 500 GHz).
AI.motivation: Previous photoconductive heterodyne demonstrations lacked proper RF IC characterization metrics such as return loss, RF/IF isolation, impedance matching, and conversion loss. This work aims to provide a validated circuit design methodology for integrated THz photonic mixers by applying standard RF integrated circuit characterization approaches to a photoconductive heterodyne mixer in monolithic form.
AI.method: A terahertz monolithic integrated circuit (TMIC) is designed combining a microcavity photoconductor with a broadband coplanar (CPW) matching network incorporating a Ti shunt resistor, an RF DC-blocking MIM capacitor, and an RF/IF decoupling capacitor. A circuit-level model including both the photoconductor and distributed CPW accesses is developed. The passive circuit is characterized up to 500 GHz using on-wafer VNA measurements, and the model is validated against measurements. Conversion loss is evaluated under illumination.
AI.result: On-wafer VNA measurements up to 500 GHz reproduce simulation accurately. The model predicts an input reflection coefficient below -10 dB up to 215 GHz and better than -6.5 dB up to 500 GHz. Measured and simulated conversion losses agree within ±1 dB over 1-500 GHz. Conversion loss is 22.5-25.5 dB below 320 GHz and 26-34 dB up to 500 GHz, demonstrating broadband operation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TMIC demonstrates broadband operation across the 1-500 GHz range and provides a validated circuit design methodology for future integrated THz photonic mixers, establishing RF IC metrics as a viable characterization framework for photoconductive heterodyne mixers.

title: Two-Parameter Ansatz for the Violation of Eigenstate Thermalization
summary: The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides the prevailing framework for understanding quantum thermalization and ergodicity in isolated many-body systems. Yet, no general theory describes the continuous onset of ETH violation between the conventional ETH and its complete breakdown. Here, we introduce a two-parameter ansatz for the ETH violation that unifies and distinguishes two mechanisms: fading ergodicity and trapped ergodicity. While fading ergodicity captures the established route to ergodicity breaking, trapped ergodicity describes a distinct scenario in which ETH is violated in finite systems but restored in the thermodynamic limit. We test this framework in the spin-1/2 $J_1$-$J_2$ chains with on-site disorder and linear potential. In both cases, we find that the observed ETH violation is consistent with trapped ergodicity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a two-parameter ansatz for eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) violation that unifies two distinct mechanisms—fading ergodicity and trapped ergodicity—and demonstrates that observed ETH violations in spin-1/2 J1-J2 chains with disorder and linear potentials are consistent with trapped ergodicity, where ETH is violated in finite systems but restored in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.motivation: While ETH provides the standard framework for understanding quantum thermalization in isolated many-body systems, there is no general theory describing the continuous onset of ETH violation between conventional ETH and its complete breakdown.
AI.method: The authors introduce a two-parameter ansatz for ETH violation that unifies and distinguishes two mechanisms: fading ergodicity (the established route to ergodicity breaking) and trapped ergodicity (where ETH is violated in finite systems but restored in the thermodynamic limit). The framework is tested on spin-1/2 J1-J2 chains with on-site disorder and a linear potential.
AI.result: In both test cases (spin-1/2 J1-J2 chains with on-site disorder and linear potential), the observed ETH violation is found to be consistent with trapped ergodicity rather than fading ergodicity.
AI.conclusion: The two-parameter ansatz provides a unified framework for characterizing the continuous onset of ETH violation, and the studied models exhibit trapped ergodicity—a distinct scenario where ETH breaking is a finite-size effect that vanishes in the thermodynamic limit.

title: MDArena: Evaluating Coding Agents on Realistic Molecular Dynamics Workflows
summary: Accelerating scientific discovery is among the most consequential applications of AI, and computational biomolecular simulation stands out as a particularly promising target within this broader effort. Coding agents promise to automate significant portions of this workflow, yet their reliability on realistic molecular dynamics (MD) tasks remains poorly characterized. To address this issue, we introduce MDArena, a benchmark of 50 containerized tasks drawn from active biomolecular simulation projects, spanning 29 molecular systems and 14 broad research protocols, including trajectory analysis, complex system preparation, free-energy protocols, and enhanced sampling. We evaluate six model/harness configurations spanning Codex and OpenCode. Among the evaluated configurations, Codex GPT-5.5 at extra-high reasoning effort performs best, reaching 24/50 Strict-Pass@1 successes (48%), followed by Codex GPT-5.5 Medium with 21/50, and OpenCode Gemini Flash 3.5 with 20/50. Average correctness and process rewards are substantially higher than strict success rates across all configurations, indicating that agents frequently make meaningful partial progress but fail on the fine-grained details required for reproducible scientific workflows. Hard tasks remain largely unsolved, particularly membrane-protein system preparation and alchemical free-energy setup, both unsolved or near-unsolved by every evaluated configuration. MDArena thus exposes a substantial gap between the usefulness of coding agents as supervised assistants and their reliability as autonomous MD researchers, while providing a reproducible and extensible platform for tracking progress toward closing it.

AI.tldr: MDArena is a benchmark of 50 containerized molecular dynamics tasks drawn from active biomolecular simulation projects, spanning 29 molecular systems and 14 research protocols. Evaluating six model/harness configurations, Codex GPT-5.5 at extra-high reasoning achieves the best strict success rate (48%), but hard tasks like membrane-protein preparation and alchemical free-energy setup remain largely unsolved, revealing a gap between coding agents as supervised assistants and as autonomous MD researchers.
AI.motivation: Coding agents promise to automate significant portions of computational biomolecular simulation workflows, yet their reliability on realistic molecular dynamics tasks remains poorly characterized due to the lack of a suitable benchmark.
AI.method: The authors construct MDArena, a benchmark of 50 containerized tasks drawn from active biomolecular simulation projects spanning 29 molecular systems and 14 research protocols (trajectory analysis, complex system preparation, free-energy protocols, enhanced sampling), and evaluate six model/harness configurations spanning Codex and OpenCode.
AI.result: Codex GPT-5.5 at extra-high reasoning effort achieves the best performance at 24/50 Strict-Pass@1 (48%), followed by Codex GPT-5.5 Medium (21/50) and OpenCode Gemini Flash 3.5 (20/50). Average correctness and process rewards substantially exceed strict success rates, indicating frequent meaningful partial progress. Hard tasks, particularly membrane-protein system preparation and alchemical free-energy setup, remain unsolved or near-unsolved across all configurations.
AI.conclusion: MDArena exposes a substantial gap between the usefulness of coding agents as supervised assistants and their reliability as autonomous MD researchers, while providing a reproducible and extensible platform for tracking progress toward closing this gap.

title: Two-phonon pairing and superconductivity in $SrTiO_3$
summary: We explore the possibility that the two-phonon pairing mechanism proposed by Ngai can explain superconductivity in doped strontium titanate (STO). The two-phonon deformation potential is evaluated using two distinct theoretical estimates based on first-principles calculations and two empirical estimates based on experimental data, yielding very large values of the same order of magnitude. We derive the effective electron-electron interaction mediated by two-phonon exchange. Crucial to our computations is the strong dispersion of the involved soft phonons. Because the scale of the two-phonon interaction is much larger than the Fermi energy, the Migdal theorem does not apply. We obtain a one-loop Eliashberg equation that can be solved in the weak-coupling limit. We find that despite the significant electron-phonon matrix element, phase space considerations considerably reduce the effective coupling. A two-phonon mechanism can not be excluded based on the $T_c$ magnitude, but its value is dominated by the high-energy-frequency physics and is weakly affected by the soft-phonon behavior. The theory predicts a $T_c$ that monotonously increases with doping, which is not in accordance with the experiment. We identify the conditions for a two-phonon mechanism to be effective in other materials and discuss possible candidates.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether the two-phonon (Ngai) pairing mechanism can explain superconductivity in doped strontium titanate (STO). Using both first-principles and empirical estimates, the authors find very large two-phonon deformation potentials but show that phase-space considerations considerably reduce the effective coupling. The predicted Tc increases monotonically with doping, contradicting experiment, so the two-phonon mechanism alone cannot fully account for STO superconductivity. The conditions for an effective two-phonon mechanism in other materials are identified.
AI.motivation: To test whether the two-phonon pairing mechanism proposed by Ngai can explain the unconventional superconductivity observed in doped strontium titanate (STO), a system whose pairing mechanism remains debated.
AI.method: The two-phonon deformation potential is evaluated via two first-principles-based theoretical estimates and two empirical estimates from experimental data. The effective electron-electron interaction mediated by two-phonon exchange is derived, and because the interaction scale exceeds the Fermi energy (invalidating Migdal's theorem), a one-loop Eliashberg equation is formulated and solved in the weak-coupling limit.
AI.result: The two-phonon deformation potentials from all four estimates are very large and of similar magnitude. Despite the significant electron-phonon matrix element, phase-space restrictions substantially reduce the effective coupling. The predicted Tc is dominated by high-energy physics, weakly affected by soft phonons, and increases monotonically with doping—in disagreement with experiment.
AI.conclusion: A two-phonon mechanism cannot be excluded based on Tc magnitude alone, but the monotonic doping dependence of the predicted Tc is inconsistent with experimental observations in STO. The paper identifies the conditions under which a two-phonon mechanism could be effective in other materials and discusses potential candidate systems.

title: Particle-Vortex Duality of Hydrodynamics
summary: Equipped with the recently recognized symmetry structure of mixed states of matter and "strong-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking" (SW-SSB), we develop a quantum particle-vortex duality of emergent model-F and model-A hydrodynamics of 2d boson/rotor systems. This duality relation demonstrates that classical hydrodynamics of 2d bosons can be described in terms of the charge symmetry $U(1)_c$, but also equivalently in terms of the dual (emergent) 1-form symmetry $U(1)^{(1)}_e$, as well as $U(1)_v$ associated with the conservation of vortices. This duality provides a bridge between the hydrodynamics of matter and magnetohydrodynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a quantum particle-vortex duality for model-F and model-A hydrodynamics of 2D boson/rotor systems, leveraging recently recognized symmetry structures of mixed states of matter and "strong-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking" (SW-SSB). This duality shows that 2D boson hydrodynamics can be equivalently described via charge symmetry U(1)_c, dual emergent 1-form symmetry U(1)^{(1)}_e, or vortex-conservation symmetry U(1)_v, bridging hydrodynamics of matter with magnetohydrodynamics.
AI.motivation: To connect the recently discovered symmetry structures of mixed states (including SW-SSB) with hydrodynamics, and to establish a duality framework that links 2D boson/rotor hydrodynamics (model-F and model-A) to dual descriptions based on 1-form symmetries and vortex conservation, thereby bridging matter hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics.
AI.method: The authors employ the recently recognized symmetry structure of mixed states of matter and strong-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) to construct a quantum particle-vortex duality transformation for emergent model-F and model-A hydrodynamics of 2D boson/rotor systems.
AI.result: The proposed duality demonstrates that classical hydrodynamics of 2D bosons admits equivalent descriptions in terms of (i) charge symmetry U(1)_c, (ii) the dual emergent 1-form symmetry U(1)^{(1)}_e, and (iii) the vortex-conserving symmetry U(1)_v. This establishes a concrete bridge between matter hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics.
AI.conclusion: The particle-vortex duality, grounded in SW-SSB and mixed-state symmetry structures, provides a unified framework connecting 2D boson hydrodynamics with dual symmetry descriptions and magnetohydrodynamics, revealing deep structural connections between these seemingly different dynamical regimes.

title: A 3-D Hybrid Numerical Method for Simulating Electromagnetic Fields in Structures with Multiple Inhomogeneous Layered Media
summary: A three-dimensional (3-D) hybrid numerical method (HNM) is presented for electromagnetic scattering in structures with multiple inhomogeneous layered media coupled to an arbitrary 3-D non-layered scattering region. It integrates the 3-D numerical mode-matching (NMM) method with a tree-cotree-based mixed finite element method (MFEM). In the NMM, the fields in the 3-D layered media are reduced to a superposition of 2-D waveguide eigenmodes, while the MFEM discretizes the 3-D scattering region. The HNM thus inherits the dimensionality-reduction advantages of both conventional hybrid MM/FEM and pure NMM. Numerical experiments show that the HNM provides an effcient alternative for scattering problems involving non-layered regions embedded in layered media.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a 3D hybrid numerical method (HNM) that combines a 3D numerical mode-matching (NMM) method with a tree-cotree-based mixed finite element method (MFEM) to efficiently solve electromagnetic scattering problems involving multiple inhomogeneous layered media coupled with arbitrary 3D non-layered scattering regions.
AI.motivation: Scattering problems that involve non-layered 3D regions embedded in layered media are computationally challenging. Existing methods either suffer from high dimensionality (pure FEM) or have limitations in handling arbitrary 3D scattering regions.
