The goal is to develop a method that reduces dimensionality while maintaining flexibility and efficiency.
AI.method: The HNM integrates two approaches: (1) the 3D numerical mode-matching (NMM) method, which reduces the fields in layered media to a superposition of 2D waveguide eigenmodes, thereby reducing dimensionality; and (2) a tree-cotree-based mixed finite element method (MFEM) that discretizes the arbitrary 3D scattering region. This combination inherits dimensionality-reduction advantages from both conventional hybrid MM/FEM and pure NMM.
AI.result: Numerical experiments demonstrate that the HNM provides an efficient alternative for solving scattering problems that involve non-layered regions embedded within layered media.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 3D hybrid numerical method is an effective and efficient approach for electromagnetic scattering in structures combining layered and non-layered regions, leveraging the dimensionality reduction of mode-matching and the flexibility of mixed finite elements.

title: Magneto-oscillations, nonlinearity, and nonreciprocity of Coulomb drag in quantum circuits
summary: We consider the problem of Coulomb drag in interactively coupled quantum circuits built of adiabatic constrictions: quantum point contacts and short quantum-wire channels. The interplay of spatial confinement and magnetic field leads to a rich oscillatory response of the drag current as a function of gate voltage and magnetic field: drag peaks track the depopulation of magnetoelectric subbands, are asymptotically periodic in inverse field, and their visibility is controlled by the competition of temperature with the field-sharpened tunneling width of the constriction. We derive a closed expression for the linear drag conductance whose interaction kernel simplifies dramatically in the experimentally relevant limit of a long thermal length compared with the range of the interwire coupling, investigate the drag in the nonlinear regime, where the drag current measures the transconductance of the drive channel at any field, and discuss physically motivated models of dissipation-induced nonreciprocity of the drag signal. Extensions accounting for Zeeman splitting, interaction renormalization of the barrier transmission, backscattering at high field, and the frequency structure of the circuit coupling delineate how each mechanism imprints itself on the temperature dependence and lineshapes of the drag oscillations.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically analyzes Coulomb drag in interacting quantum circuits built from adiabatic constrictions (quantum point contacts and short quantum wires), revealing oscillatory drag responses as functions of gate voltage and magnetic field, with drag peaks tracking subband depopulation and periodic-in-inverse-field behavior. A closed expression for linear drag conductance is derived alongside analyses of nonlinear regimes, dissipation-induced nonreciprocity, and extensions addressing Zeeman splitting, barrier renormalization, high-field backscattering, and frequency-dependent coupling.
AI.motivation: To understand how Coulomb drag manifests in quantum circuits composed of adiabatic constrictions under magnetic fields, where the interplay of spatial confinement and field leads to rich oscillatory transport phenomena that are not captured by existing models.
AI.method: The authors derive a closed-form expression for the linear drag conductance, simplify the interaction kernel in the limit where thermal length far exceeds the interwire coupling range, and extend the analysis to the nonlinear regime (where drag current measures transconductance) and to models of dissipation-induced nonreciprocity. Additional extensions cover Zeeman splitting, interaction renormalization of barrier transmission, high-field backscattering, and frequency structure of circuit coupling.
AI.result: Drag peaks track magnetoelectric subband depopulation, exhibit asymptotic periodicity in inverse magnetic field, and their visibility is governed by the competition between temperature and the field-sharpened tunneling width of the constriction. The analysis reveals how each physical mechanism (Zeeman splitting, interaction renormalization, backscattering, coupling frequencies) imprints distinct signatures on the temperature dependence and lineshapes of the drag oscillations.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a comprehensive theoretical description of Coulomb drag in adiabatic-constriction quantum circuits, bridging linear and nonlinear regimes and identifying how various microscopic mechanisms shape the observable oscillatory drag signatures in both gate voltage and magnetic field.

title: Symmetry-Guided Computational Screening of Two-Dimensional Altermagnets with ab initio Hubbard Corrections
summary: Altermagnets combine compensated antiferromagnetic order with momentum-dependent spin splitting, offering a promising platform for spintronic applications without macroscopic magnetization or stray magnetic fields. Although a wide range of three-dimensional (3D) materials have been identified as altermagnets, two-dimensional (2D) altermagnets remain comparatively limited. In this work, we perform a high-throughput computational search for altermagnetism across 2710 materials in the Materials Cloud 2D Crystals (MC2D) database. Our approach combines symmetry-based screening with first-principles density functional theory calculations, including self-consistent Hubbard-$U$ corrections, to reliably capture magnetic ground states. Through a systematic exploration of magnetic configurations and their energetic stability, we identify 42 materials exhibiting altermagnetic ground states for at least one value of $U$, of which 24 remain robust upon determination of the Hubbard-$U$ parameters from first principles--including 4 materials previously reported in the literature and 20 newly predicted candidates. These comprise promising monolayers such as metallic Fe$_2$Si$_2$SbO$_9$, and insulating CoBrO, with spin splittings about 294 meV and 330 meV, respectively. Our results significantly expand the pool of potential 2D altermagnet candidates with favorable exfoliation energetics and provide valuable guidance for experimental efforts. In addition, this work establishes a high-throughput computational framework for reproducible discovery and characterization of altermagnetic materials.

AI.tldr: A high-throughput computational search identifies 24 robust two-dimensional altermagnetic materials (including 20 new candidates) from 2710 materials in the MC2D database, using symmetry-based screening combined with DFT+U calculations, significantly expanding the pool of 2D altermagnet candidates.
AI.motivation: While three-dimensional altermagnets are well-established, the number of 2D altermagnetic materials remains limited. The authors aim to expand the pool of 2D altermagnet candidates through a systematic high-throughput search, which is important for spintronic applications that benefit from the absence of macroscopic magnetization and stray fields.
AI.method: The authors perform a high-throughput computational search across 2710 materials in the Materials Cloud 2D Crystals (MC2D) database. They combine symmetry-based screening with first-principles density functional theory calculations, including self-consistent Hubbard-U corrections, to reliably capture magnetic ground states. They systematically explore magnetic configurations and their energetic stability, and determine Hubbard-U parameters from first principles for robustness assessment.
AI.result: The search identified 42 materials with altermagnetic ground states for at least one value of U, with 24 remaining robust after first-principles Hubbard-U determination—4 previously reported and 20 newly predicted. Notable candidates include metallic Fe$_2$Si$_2$SbO$_9$ with spin splitting of ~294 meV and insulating CoBrO with ~330 meV spin splitting.
AI.conclusion: The results significantly expand the available pool of 2D altermagnet candidates with favorable exfoliation energetics, provide guidance for experimental efforts, and establish a reproducible high-throughput computational framework for discovering and characterizing altermagnetic materials.

title: Surface Variables Description of Axion Topological Materials
summary: We study the response of axion topological materials under the presence of external static electric and magnetic fields. We focus on the macroscopic quasi-static magnetoelectric response of topological insulators. We use techniques based on surface variables that have been previously employed in soft condensed matter problems for the description of heterogeneous systems composed of multiple homogeneous materials. A complete description of the whole system is written in terms of surface degrees of freedom, which in this case correspond to effective surface charge and surface current densities. We obtain a set of integral equations satisfied by these variables. We present exact analytic solutions for axial-symmetric cases. We develop a numerical method for the solution of the integral equations by means of a boundary finite element method. We apply the numerical method to topological insulators with different geometries such as spheres, hollow spheres and toroidal surfaces. We show that that a variational principle can be used to recover the surface variables equations.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the macroscopic quasi-static magnetoelectric response of axion topological materials under external static electric and magnetic fields using surface variables (effective surface charge and current densities), deriving integral equations, analytic solutions for axial-symmetric cases, and a boundary finite element method for arbitrary geometries including spheres, hollow spheres, and tori. A variational principle is shown to recover the surface equations.
AI.motivation: To provide a complete and computationally tractable description of the macroscopic magnetoelectric response of topological insulators, particularly for arbitrary geometries where existing methods are insufficient.
AI.method: The authors employ surface variables (effective surface charge and surface current densities), a technique borrowed from soft condensed matter physics for heterogeneous systems. They derive a set of integral equations for these surface variables, present exact analytic solutions for axial-symmetric cases, and develop a boundary finite element method for numerical solution. The method is applied to spheres, hollow spheres, and toroidal geometries.
AI.result: Exact analytic solutions are obtained for axial-symmetric configurations, and a numerical boundary finite element method is developed and applied to topological insulators with spherical, hollow spherical, and toroidal geometries. A variational principle is also shown to recover the surface variable integral equations.
AI.conclusion: The surface-variable approach provides a complete and general framework for computing the quasi-static magnetoelectric response of topological insulators of arbitrary geometry, validated by analytic solutions in symmetric cases and demonstrated numerically for complex geometries.

title: The Existence Regions for Transcomplex Recombination of Heavy Ions. Two-Dimensional Recombination Regions and Surroundings Indices
comment: 52 pages, 14 figures, a somewhat abridged version of the article was published in Russian Journal of Physical Chemistry B
summary: In this paper, we examine transcomplex recombination RCs$^+$ + Br$^-$ $\to$ CsBr + R (R = Kr, Xe, Hg) for collision energies from 0.1 to 2.5 eV. Within the framework of the quasiclassical trajectory method on semiempirical diabatic potential energy surfaces, we have considered the existence regions for recombination in the space of kinematic parameters. Two-dimensional "slices" of the existence regions for recombination (on the sphere where the coordinates are the orientation angles of the initial direction of the axis of the ionic complex RCs$^+$) sometimes exhibit a chaotic structure. We have proposed a quantitative measure of chaoticity of two-dimensional existence regions for recombination (on the basis of the combinatorics of matrices of zeros and ones) and have presented examples of chaotic regions. We have introduced the surroundings index of recombinative trajectories and have explored its connection with the integration time of the trajectory and with the total internal energy of the product molecule CsBr.

AI.tldr: This paper studies transcomplex recombination reactions RCs⁺ + Br⁻ → CsBr + R (R = Kr, Xe, Hg) at collision energies 0.1–2.5 eV using quasiclassical trajectory methods on semiempirical diabatic potential energy surfaces, examining the structure of recombination existence regions, introducing a quantitative chaos measure based on zero-one combinatorics, and defining a surroundings index linking trajectory integration time to product internal energy.
AI.motivation: To understand the kinematic parameter space structure for transcomplex recombination processes and quantify chaotic behavior in the existence regions of recombination, providing deeper insight into the dynamics of barrierless ion-molecule recombination collisions.
AI.method: Quasiclassical trajectory method (QCT) on semiempirical diabatic potential energy surfaces; two-dimensional slice analysis of existence regions on orientation-angle spheres; a combinatorial measure of chaoticity based on zero-one matrices; and a surroundings index for recombinative trajectories correlated with integration time and product internal energy.
AI.result: Two-dimensional slices of recombination existence regions exhibit chaotic structures for certain orientation angles; a quantitative chaos measure successfully identifies such chaotic regions; the surroundings index correlates with integration time and total internal energy of the CsBr product.
AI.conclusion: Transcomplex recombination regions can exhibit pronounced chaotic structure in kinematic parameter space, and the proposed quantitative tools (chaoticity measure and surroundings index) effectively characterize these dynamics and their relation to product energy content.

title: Thermodynamic phase transition, pairing symmetry and Fermi surface topology in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelate films
summary: Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates provide an uncharted territory to explore high-transition-temperature (high-$T_C$) superconductivity and superconducting mechanism. Here, we investigate the electronic structure of a new type of high-$T_C$ superconducting RP nickelate heterostructure $\mathrm{La_2PrNi_2O_7/NdAlO_3}$ by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. A superconducting state is observed without a pseudogap state, enabling a direct measurement of the superconducting order parameter and a microscopic extraction of the electronic specific heat. The observed superconducting gap opens at $T_C$ with prominent coherence peaks, illustrating the emergence of nonzero order parameter upon entering the superconducting state. An electronic specific heat jump appears at $T_C$, further demonstrating a thermodynamic phase transition. The magnitude of the superconducting order parameter is quantified by the observed superconducting coherence peaks, and a nodeless behavior is unambiguously established in the absence of pseudogap. The underlying Fermi surface consists of $α$, $β$ and $γ$ pockets, exhibiting a multi-orbital nature. Strain dependent measurements further reveal the $γ$ pocket in all superconducting and non-superconducting films with different epitaxial strain. Our results establish the missing thermodynamic evidence for superconducting phase transition in nickelates. They also provide direct evidence for the symmetry of the superconducting order parameter and illustrate the relationship between Fermi surface topology and the emergence of superconductivity in RP nickelate films.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the electronic structure of a new high-Tc superconducting Ruddlesden-Popper nickelate heterostructure La2PrNi2O7/NdAlO3 using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, directly measuring the superconducting order parameter and electronic specific heat without a pseudogap state, establishing thermodynamic evidence for the superconducting phase transition and revealing a nodeless order parameter with multi-orbital Fermi surface topology.
AI.motivation: RP nickelates represent an unexplored frontier for high-Tc superconductivity research. Prior studies lacked direct thermodynamic evidence for the superconducting phase transition and unambiguous determination of the superconducting order parameter symmetry, partly due to the presence of pseudogap states obscuring measurements.
AI.method: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) was used to study the electronic structure of La2PrNi2O7/NdAlO3 heterostructure films. The superconducting gap was measured directly in the absence of a pseudogap, enabling extraction of the electronic specific heat microscopically. Strain-dependent measurements compared superconducting and non-superconducting films across different epitaxial strains.
AI.result: A superconducting gap opens at Tc with prominent coherence peaks, demonstrating nonzero order parameter formation. An electronic specific heat jump appears at Tc, confirming a thermodynamic phase transition. The order parameter is nodeless, quantified from coherence peaks. The Fermi surface consists of α, β, and γ pockets (multi-orbital), with the γ pocket present in all films regardless of superconducting state or epitaxial strain.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the missing thermodynamic evidence for the superconducting phase transition in nickelates, offers direct evidence for the symmetry (nodeless) of the superconducting order parameter, and clarifies the connection between Fermi surface topology and superconductivity in RP nickelate films.

title: Large scale neural quantum states reveal the interplay between superconductivity and quantum criticality in the Hofstadter-Hubbard model
summary: Understanding how a parent insulating state shapes the superconductivity that emerges upon doping is a long-standing problem dating back to Anderson's resonating-valence-bond proposal. The triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model with $π/2$ flux per plaquette offers an ideal setting for this question: at half filling it hosts two distinct parent states---an integer quantum Hall insulator at weak coupling and a chiral spin liquid at intermediate coupling---separated by a topological phase transition. Using neural quantum states on tori of up to $432$ sites, we present strong evidence that the transition is continuous, with a vanishing $2e$ charge gap and critical charge fluctuations. Upon doping, we find a topological superconductor with off-diagonal long-range order consistent with $d+id$ pairing on either side of the transition. The two ingredients of superconductivity, pair formation and phase coherence, respond to the parent state in sharply different ways: while the pairing order parameter remains nearly unchanged across the transition, the superfluid stiffness is strongly enhanced near the critical point. The energy scale of the superconductor is therefore set not by which parent state is doped, but by proximity to the transition between them. Our results establish neural quantum states as a powerful tool for understanding the delicate interplay between long-ranged electronic correlations and superconductivity.

AI.tldr: Using neural quantum states on large tori (up to 432 sites), this paper studies the Hofstadter-Hubbard model with π/2 flux per plaquette, showing a continuous topological phase transition between an integer quantum Hall insulator and a chiral spin liquid at half filling. Upon doping, a d+id topological superconductor emerges on both sides of the transition, with pairing order nearly unchanged while superfluid stiffness peaks near the critical point, revealing that superconducting energy scales are set by proximity to the parent-state transition rather than which parent state is doped.
AI.motivation: Understanding how the parent insulating state shapes emergent superconductivity upon doping is a long-standing problem dating back to Anderson's resonating-valence-bond proposal. The triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model with π/2 flux provides an ideal setting because it hosts two distinct parent states (an integer quantum Hall insulator at weak coupling and a chiral spin liquid at intermediate coupling) separated by a topological phase transition, allowing direct investigation of how the parent state influences superconductivity.
AI.method: The authors employ neural quantum states (neural network-based variational wavefunctions) on tori of up to 432 sites to simulate the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model with π/2 flux per plaquette at and away from half filling. They compute the 2e charge gap, charge fluctuations, pairing order parameters, and superfluid stiffness to characterize both the parent-state transition and the emergent superconducting phases.
AI.result: The transition between the integer quantum Hall insulator and chiral spin liquid is continuous, characterized by a vanishing 2e charge gap and critical charge fluctuations. Upon doping, a topological superconductor with d+id pairing off-diagonal long-range order appears on both sides of the transition. The pairing order parameter remains nearly unchanged across the transition, while the superfluid stiffness is strongly enhanced near the critical point.
AI.conclusion: The energy scale of the superconductor is determined not by which parent state is doped, but by proximity to the transition between them. This work also establishes neural quantum states as a powerful computational tool for studying the delicate interplay between long-ranged electronic correlations and superconductivity.

title: AccelNet: Exact backward-compatible acceleration of polynomial angular descriptors through Cartesian moment factorization
summary: We present AccelNet, an exact, backward-compatible method for accelerating existing trained aenet and n2p2 neural-network potentials without retraining. For angular terms with separable one-neighbor weights and a finite polynomial dependence on $\cos θ$, the method exploits their hidden finite-rank structure to replace explicit neighbor-pair loops by one-neighbor Cartesian moments. AccelNet reads models trained with either package and reproduces their descriptors, energies, and analytic forces to floating-point roundoff. We verified this equivalence for H$_2$O and TiO$_2$ models and tested the resulting potentials in LAMMPS molecular-dynamics simulations. The implementation, model-conversion tools, and LAMMPS interfaces are released as open-source software.

AI.tldr: AccelNet is an exact, backward-compatible acceleration method for existing aenet and n2p2 neural-network potentials that exploits the hidden finite-rank structure of angular terms to replace expensive neighbor-pair loops with one-neighbor Cartesian moments, reproducing energies and forces to floating-point roundoff without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing trained aenet and n2p2 neural-network potentials are computationally expensive due to explicit neighbor-pair loops in angular terms, motivating an acceleration approach that does not require retraining and remains backward-compatible with already-trained models.
AI.method: AccelNet exploits the hidden finite-rank structure of angular terms that have separable one-neighbor weights and a finite polynomial dependence on cos θ, replacing explicit neighbor-pair loops with one-neighbor Cartesian moments to accelerate computations.
AI.result: AccelNet reproduces descriptors, energies, and analytic forces to floating-point roundoff compared to original aenet and n2p2 models, verified for H₂O and TiO₂ models within LAMMPS molecular-dynamics simulations.
AI.conclusion: The exact and backward-compatible acceleration method is validated and released as open-source software including model-conversion tools and LAMMPS interfaces.

title: Two dimensional inhomogeneous classical systems at criticality
summary: We study simple inhomogeneous deformations of known two-dimensional classical lattice models described by conformal field theory (CFT) at large distances. The deformations are chosen to vary slowly at lattice scales, while preserving critical behavior. Globally, we find that such systems are described by a CFT in curved space, and identify the underlying space metric. Our two examples are the Ising model and the six vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions. In the latter boundaries are also inhomogeneous, which complicates the analysis. We nevertheless solve the free case using hydrodynamics. In the presence of interactions we determine the arctic curve which separates a critical fluctuating region from an ordered (frozen) phase.

AI.tldr: This paper studies slowly-varying inhomogeneous deformations of two-dimensional classical lattice models (Ising model and six-vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions) at criticality, showing they are described by CFT in curved space and identifying the underlying space metric, with the free case solved via hydrodynamics and the interacting case yielding an arctic curve separating critical from frozen regions.
AI.motivation: To understand how inhomogeneously deformed critical lattice models behave at large scales, characterization of the induced curved-space CFT describing these systems, and determination of phase-separation boundaries in interacting models.
AI.method: The authors consider lattice deformations that vary slowly relative to lattice scales while preserving critical behavior, and study two canonical examples—the Ising model and the six-vertex model with (inhomogeneous) domain wall boundary conditions. The free case is solved via hydrodynamic methods, while interacting cases are analyzed to determine the arctic curve separating critical and frozen regions.
AI.result: The systems are globally described by CFT in curved space, with an explicit identification of the underlying space metric. For the six-vertex model with domain wall boundaries, the free case is solved using hydrodynamics, and for interacting cases the arctic curve separating the critical fluctuating region from the ordered frozen phase is determined.
AI.conclusion: Slow, criticality-preserving inhomogeneous deformations of 2D lattice models yield curved-space CFT descriptions, and the arctic curve methodology successfully captures phase boundaries in interacting inhomogeneous six-vertex systems.

title: Lifshitz transitions and isospin polarization in twist-decoupled monolayer-bilayer graphene
summary: Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene (BLG) hosts correlated electronic phases tied to low-energy Lifshitz transitions at saddle points in its valence band. To access this regime, ultralow charge disorder and control over a vertical electric field are simultaneously required. Here, we employ a twist-decoupled monolayer (MLG) to bias a proximal BLG in the absence of an external displacement field (D). We thereby reveal three-fold degenerate quantum Hall states at D = 0, with multiple transitions driven by doping, magnetic and electric field. Spontaneous broken symmetry in the vicinity of the valence band edge is signaled by the emergence of quantum oscillations with anomalous frequencies and large quasiparticle mass. These results indicate that electronic interactions in BLG are preserved in presence of an atomically close MLG, while showcasing the potential of CVD-grown graphene multilayers for the exploration of correlated phases of matter.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that using a twist-decoupled monolayer graphene as a local gate to bias proximal Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene reveals three-fold degenerate quantum Hall states at zero displacement field, with spontaneous broken symmetry near the valence band edge indicated by anomalous quantum oscillation frequencies and large quasiparticle mass, showing electronic interactions are preserved and highlighting CVD-grown graphene multilayers for studying correlated phases.
AI.motivation: Accessing correlated electronic phases in Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene requires simultaneously achieving ultralow charge disorder and vertical electric field control. This is experimentally challenging, motivating a new approach to study the low-energy Lifshitz transitions without an external displacement field.
AI.method: The authors employ a twist-decoupled monolayer graphene to bias a proximal bilayer graphene in the absence of an external displacement field (D = 0), then probe quantum Hall states and quantum oscillations as a function of doping, magnetic field, and electric field.
AI.result: They observe three-fold degenerate quantum Hall states at D = 0 with multiple transitions driven by doping, magnetic, and electric fields. Anomalous quantum oscillation frequencies and large quasiparticle mass reveal spontaneous broken symmetry near the valence band edge, demonstrating preserved electronic interactions in BLG despite the atomically close MLG.
AI.conclusion: Electronic interactions in bilayer graphene are preserved in the presence of a proximal monolayer graphene, and CVD-grown graphene multilayers offer a promising platform for exploring correlated phases of matter.

title: Optical properties of Ag, Au, and Cu from first principles
summary: We present a comprehensive framework for investigating the optical response of metals from first principles that combines density functional theory, many-body perturbation theory, and efficient interpolation techniques based on maximally localized Wannier functions, and apply it to analyze the optical properties of silver (Ag), gold (Au), and copper (Cu). We evaluate the optical properties of these metallic materials considering both single-particle direct and phonon-assisted excitations, as well as the resistive Drude contribution. We find an overall excellent agreement with experimental optical measurements for these materials, and show that both single-particle and collective excitations are important in capturing their optical response in the infrared. Our methodology provides fundamental understanding of the optical response of metals and is generally applicable to investigate the optoelectronic properties of emerging metallic materials.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a first-principles framework combining density functional theory, many-body perturbation theory, and Wannier function interpolation to compute the optical response of metals. Applied to silver, gold, and copper, the framework includes single-particle, phonon-assisted, and Drude contributions, achieving excellent agreement with experimental optical measurements.
AI.motivation: There is a need for a comprehensive and accurate first-principles methodology to understand the optical response of metals, particularly in the infrared, where both single-particle and collective excitations play important roles.
AI.method: The framework combines density functional theory, many-body perturbation theory, and maximally localized Wannier function-based interpolation techniques to evaluate optical properties of metals, considering single-particle direct excitations, phonon-assisted excitations, and the resistive Drude contribution.
AI.result: The framework achieves excellent agreement with experimental optical measurements for silver, gold, and copper, demonstrating that both single-particle and collective excitations are necessary to accurately capture the optical response in the infrared region.
AI.conclusion: The methodology provides fundamental understanding of metal optical response and is generally applicable to investigating the optoelectronic properties of emerging metallic materials beyond noble metals.

title: Experimental access to molarity's blind spot in macroscopic assays
comment: 58 pages, 6 figures. Companion paper submitted simultaneously: "A concentration-independent paradigm rendering weak interactions inherently quantifiable" (M. Yoshimura et al.). Cross-references to the companion arXiv identifier will be added in v2
summary: Chemical kinetics has long inferred local molecular behaviour through the flask-and-molarity pairing, where well-mixed concentrations serve as the experimental readout. Yet many biological reactions occur in structured environments. Researchers have long recognized that concentration may not carry the same operational meaning in such environments, but even local concepts such as effective molarity usually translate local effects back into a single value with units of concentration. What has been missing is the complementary path: a bench-compatible way to make local structure an experimental variable, rather than only a correction to molarity. Here we show a chemistry-geometry crossover that the flask-and-molarity interface could not make visible. In the micromolar-or-weaker affinity regime, inhibition can switch sharply out of the familiar concentration-and-affinity mode: chemical binding strength no longer determines the response, and the shape of the target's local space does. A bench-compatible interface made this switch measurable by separating bulk dose from local geometry. This blind spot arose from the hidden premise that macroscopic pooling makes a structured local state readable as a single local concentration. The chemistry-geometry crossover breaks that premise: in a structured target environment, a macroscopic assay can remain sensitive to the probability distribution of local states, so collapsing that distribution to one concentration-valued number removes the geometric control axis from the readout. By preserving that axis in the experiment, the interface bypasses molarity's hidden bottleneck and provides a routine experimental route to remeasure and reinterpret molecular interactions in structured space.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a chemistry-geometry crossover in micromolar-or-weaker affinity regimes where inhibition response is determined by the shape of the target's local space rather than chemical binding strength, breaking the traditional flask-and-molarity paradigm. A bench-compatible interface separating bulk dose from local geometry makes this switch measurable and provides a routine route to reinterpret molecular interactions in structured environments.
AI.motivation: Traditional chemical kinetics relies on the flask-and-molarity pairing where well-mixed concentrations serve as the experimental readout. However, many biological reactions occur in structured environments where concentration may not carry the same operational meaning. The missing piece is a bench-compatible way to make local structure an experimental variable rather than only a correction to molarity—the complementary path that would make local geometry directly observable.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate a chemistry-geometry crossover where inhibition switches out of the familiar concentration-and-affinity mode into a regime where the shape of the target's local space determines the response. They developed a bench-compatible interface that separates bulk dose from local geometry, preserving the geometric control axis in the experimental readout rather than collapsing the probability distribution of local states into a single concentration-valued number.
AI.result: In the micromolar-or-weaker affinity regime, inhibition can switch sharply such that chemical binding strength no longer determines response—local geometry does. The macroscopic assay remains sensitive to the probability distribution of local states in structured target environments, making the chemistry-geometry crossover visible through the new interface where conventional molarity-based approaches could not.
AI.conclusion: The flask-and-molarity interface has a hidden bottleneck: collapsing the local state distribution to one concentration removes the geometric control axis from the readout. By preserving that axis, the new interface bypasses molarity's limitation and provides a routine experimental route to remeasure and reinterpret molecular interactions in structured space.

title: Tunable Skyrmions in a Topological Wigner Crystal
summary: In low density systems with strong interactions electrons are expected to crystallize into a Wigner solid. Recently, advances in two-dimensional systems where electrons carry Berry curvature have added a topological dimension to Wigner crystallization. Using a model for pseudospin interactions in a topological Wigner crystal, here we show that the competition between ferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange $J$ and the chiral interaction $γ$ on the triangular lattice stabilizes a zero-field skyrmion crystal whose density is continuously tunable through the ratio $γ/J$. The chiral interaction originates from finite Berry curvature in an underlying time-reversal broken Wigner crystal. In the continuum limit, the chiral interaction acts as a chemical potential for skyrmions, while higher-order gradient terms beyond the nonlinear sigma model select the skyrmion density. At large chiral coupling, we uncover a 24-site tetra-skyrmion crystal carrying four units of topological charge per magnetic unit cell, which becomes degenerate with four-sublattice tetrahedral order as $J \to 0$. We characterize the magnon structure for these phases and discuss the transition between the tunable skyrmion crystal to these states at large $γ/J$. Our results establish the phase diagram of ferromagnetic topological Wigner crystals.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a ferromagnetic topological Wigner crystal where competition between Heisenberg exchange J and chiral interaction γ stabilizes a zero-field skyrmion crystal with continuously tunable density (γ/J). At large chiral coupling, a 24-site tetra-skyrmion crystal emerges, becoming degenerate with tetrahedral order as J→0. The work establishes the full phase diagram of ferromagnetic topological Wigner crystals.
AI.motivation: Electrons in low-density strongly interacting systems are expected to form Wigner crystals. Recent advances in 2D systems with Berry curvature add a topological dimension to Wigner crystallization, and the authors aim to understand new topological phases (e.g., skyrmion crystals) that emerge from this interplay.
AI.method: The authors use a model for pseudospin interactions in a topological Wigner crystal on the triangular lattice, analyzing the competition between ferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange J and a chiral interaction γ arising from finite Berry curvature in a time-reversal broken Wigner crystal. They analyze the continuum limit (where the chiral interaction acts as a chemical potential for skyrmions) and higher-order gradient terms beyond the nonlinear sigma model to determine skyrmion density selection. Magnon structure characterization is also performed.
AI.result: The competition between J and γ stabilizes a zero-field skyrmion crystal with density tunable through γ/J. At large γ, a 24-site tetra-skyrmion crystal carrying 4 units of topological charge per magnetic unit cell is found, which becomes degenerate with four-sublattice tetrahedral order as J→0. The magnon structure of these phases is characterized, and the transition between the tunable skyrmion crystal and the large-γ/J states is discussed.
AI.conclusion: The results establish the phase diagram of ferromagnetic topological Wigner crystals, demonstrating that Berry curvature-induced chiral interactions can stabilize tunable skyrmion crystals in zero field, with a rich set of topological phases at strong chiral coupling.

title: Epitaxial SiGeSn alloys for CMOS-compatible thermoelectric devices
summary: The integration of thermoelectric devices into mainstream microelectronic technological platform could be a major breakthrough in various fields within the \emph{so-called} Green-IT realm. In this article, the thermoelectric properties of heteroepitaxial SiGeSn alloys, a novel CMOS compatible material system, are evaluated to assess their possible application in thermoelectric devices. To this purpose, starting from the experimentally low lattice thermal conductivity of SiGeSn/Ge/Si layers of about $\sim$1-2 W/m$\cdot$K assessed by means of 3-$ω$ measurements, the figure of merits are calculated through the use of Boltzmann transport equation, taking into account the relevant inter-valley scattering processes, peculiar of this multi-valley material system. Values for the figure of merit $ZT$ exceeding $1$ have been obtained for both p- and n- type material at operating temperatures within the 300---400 K range, i.e. at a typical On-Chip temperatures. In this interval, the predicted power factor also features very competitive values of the order of 20 $\rm{μW/cm\cdot K^2}$. Our finding indicates that this new class of Si-based materials has extremely good prospects for real-world applications, and can further stimulate scientific investigation in this ambit.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the thermoelectric properties of heteroepitaxial SiGeSn alloys, a CMOS-compatible material system, and predicts figure of merit (ZT) values exceeding 1 for both p- and n-type materials at typical on-chip temperatures (300–400 K), with competitive power factors around 20 μW/cm·K², indicating strong potential for thermoelectric device applications in Green-IT.
AI.motivation: To assess whether SiGeSn alloys, a novel CMOS-compatible material system, can be integrated into mainstream microelectronic platforms for thermoelectric applications, potentially advancing the Green-IT field by enabling on-chip thermal energy harvesting and management.
AI.method: Starting from experimentally measured low lattice thermal conductivity of SiGeSn/Ge/Si layers (~1-2 W/m·K) obtained via 3-ω measurements, the figure of merit was calculated using Boltzmann transport equation, explicitly accounting for inter-valley scattering processes characteristic of this multi-valley material system.
AI.result: Figure of merit ZT exceeding 1 was obtained for both p- and n-type materials at operating temperatures of 300–400 K (typical on-chip temperatures), with predicted power factors around 20 μW/cm·K².
AI.conclusion: SiGeSn alloys show extremely good prospects for real-world thermoelectric applications as a new class of Si-based CMOS-compatible materials, warranting further scientific investigation in this area.

title: Exact Resonances Are Not Sufficient for Phonon Energy Diffusion
summary: Multi-phonon resonance conditions underpin kinetic theories of phonon transport and lattice thermalization. We show that exact resonance matching, nonzero interaction coefficients, and network connectivity do not guarantee persistent energy diffusion. Symmetry-enforced balance relations drive exact-resonant collision currents to nonthermal zero-flux states, producing kinetic arrest from individual resonant sets to connected networks. Complete energy spreading is sustained by quasi-resonances. The thermodynamic and weak-nonlinearity limits do not commute: the leading kinetic behavior is recovered in the former, whereas at fixed finite size the thermalization time diverges through higher-order crossovers as the nonlinearity vanishes. Exact-resonance existence and connectivity are therefore kinematic, not sufficient dynamical, criteria for phonon energy diffusion.

AI.tldr: Exact multi-phonon resonances do not guarantee energy diffusion in lattice systems despite satisfying standard kinetic criteria. Symmetry-enforced balance relations drive exact-resonant collision currents to nonthermal zero-flux states, causing kinetic arrest. Quasi-resonances are what sustain complete energy spreading, and the thermodynamic and weak-nonlinearity limits do not commute.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to challenge the prevailing assumption in kinetic theories of phonon transport that exact resonance matching, nonzero interaction coefficients, and network connectivity are sufficient to guarantee persistent energy diffusion. They seek to establish the actual dynamical criteria for phonon energy diffusion.
AI.method: The study analyzes exact-resonant collision currents in multi-phonon systems, examining symmetry-enforced balance relations and their effect on energy flow. It compares exact resonances against quasi-resonances and investigates the interplay between thermodynamic limits and weak-nonlinearity limits, including higher-order crossover scaling analyses at fixed finite system sizes.
AI.result: Exact-resonant collision currents converge to nonthermal zero-flux states due to symmetry-enforced balance relations, producing kinetic arrest across individual resonant sets and connected networks. Quasi-resonances sustain complete energy spreading. The thermodynamic and weak-nonlinearity limits do not commute: kinetic behavior is recovered in the thermodynamic limit, while at fixed finite size thermalization time diverges through higher-order crossovers as nonlinearity vanishes.
AI.conclusion: Exact-resonance existence and network connectivity are merely kinematic criteria, not sufficient dynamical conditions for phonon energy diffusion. The symmetry-enforced balance mechanism explains kinetic arrest, and quasi-resonances—not exact resonances—are the drivers of persistent energy spreading.

title: Chaos and Diffusion in Twisted Bilayer Graphene
summary: We numerically analyze chaos and diffusion in experimentally-relevant models of twisted bilayer graphene. Our results indicate that finite systems at both commensurate and incommensurate rotation angles exhibit chaos. We compute the Thouless energy of the system at intermediate twist angles to further understand the diffusive processes associated with the chaotic nature of the spectrum. We find that the mean free path of the non-interacting electrons scales with the system size, which is consistent with diffusive processes caused by border-induced scattering. In summary, our results show the role of borders as a experimentally relevant single-particle scattering mechanism, which is much stronger than in single-layer graphene and induces chaos and diffusion regardless of the rotation angle and the lattice commensurability.

AI.tldr: Using numerical analysis, the authors study chaos and diffusion in twisted bilayer graphene models. They find that finite systems exhibit chaos at both commensurate and incommensurate rotation angles. The mean free path of non-interacting electrons scales with system size, consistent with border-induced diffusive scattering. Borders are shown to be a much stronger single-particle scattering mechanism than in single-layer graphene, inducing chaos and diffusion independent of twist angle or lattice commensurability.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of system borders as a single-particle scattering mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene, and to determine whether chaos and diffusion arise regardless of twist angle and lattice commensurability—an experimentally relevant question that goes beyond the well-studied single-layer graphene case.
AI.method: The authors perform numerical simulations of chaos and diffusion in finite models of twisted bilayer graphene at both commensurate and incommensurate rotation angles. They compute the Thouless energy at intermediate twist angles to analyze diffusive processes linked to the chaotic spectrum, and extract the mean free path scaling with system size.
AI.result: Finite twisted bilayer graphene systems exhibit chaos at all studied rotation angles (commensurate and incommensurate). The mean free path of non-interacting electrons scales with system size, indicating border-induced diffusive scattering. Border scattering is significantly stronger than in single-layer graphene.
AI.conclusion: System borders serve as a robust and experimentally relevant single-particle scattering mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene, inducing chaos and diffusion regardless of rotation angle or lattice commensurability. This highlights the importance of finite-size/boundary effects in experimental realizations of twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Electrostatic Superlattices beyond 1:1 Stoichiometry
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. The Supporting Information file is uploaded as ancillary file
summary: Exotic nanoparticle superstructures can be accessed by harnessing nanoparticle softness and charge regulation, features often viewed as obstacles to structural control. Here, we show that regulated charge mismatch in polymer-grafted nanoparticles enables the assembly of high-stoichiometry cubic superlattices. By co-tuning grafting density, particle size, and bulk composition, we realize ionic-lattice analogues such as CaF2 and Th3P4, as well as single-component A3 and A7 superlattices without atomic counterparts. The A3 lattice has recently been identified theoretically as a photonic band-gap lattice. These phases emerge from a 1:1 "parent" lattice when local charge neutrality cannot be satisfied, driving either progressive interstitial filling or reorganization into a larger basis. For instance, the systematic occupation of ZnS tetrahedral sites yields CaF2, while ligand-swapping symmetry breaking converts CsCl into Th3P4. Upon heating, the assemblies exhibit reversible lattice contraction and pronounced negative thermal expansion. Furthermore, the energetic penalty for defects increases with nanoparticle size, facilitating the scalable production of high-quality, open superlattices for photonic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that regulated charge mismatch in polymer-grafted nanoparticles enables the assembly of high-stoichiometry cubic superlattices, including ionic-lattice analogues (CaF2, Th3P4) and novel single-component A3 and A7 lattices. These phases emerge when local charge neutrality in a 1:1 parent lattice cannot be satisfied, driving structural reorganization. The assemblies exhibit reversible lattice contraction and negative thermal expansion, with defect penalties increasing with particle size for scalable production of open superlattices for photonic applications.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to leverage nanoparticle softness and charge regulation—typically seen as obstacles to structural control—as tools to access exotic symmetry lattices, particularly high-stoichiometry cubic superlattices unattainable with conventional hard-particle assembly.
AI.method: The approach co-tunes grafting density, particle size, and bulk composition to regulate charge mismatch in polymer-grafted nanoparticles. Structural transitions are driven by local charge-neutrality frustration in a 1:1 parent lattice, leading to either progressive interstitial filling (yielding CaF2) or ligand-swapping symmetry breaking (converting CsCl into Th3P4).
AI.result: The authors successfully realize ionic-lattice analogues (CaF2, Th3P4) and single-component A3/A7 superlattices, including the theoretically predicted photonic band-gap A3 lattice. The assemblies show reversible lattice contraction and pronounced negative thermal expansion upon heating, and increasing particle size raises the energetic penalty for defects, improving crystal quality.
AI.conclusion: Charge-regulated softness in polymer-grafted nanoparticles is a powerful and tunable design principle for assembling high-stoichiometry cubic superlattices with non-trivial symmetries, offering a scalable route to high-quality open lattices with promising photonic properties.

title: Picometre-scale real-time drift correction in TEM and STEM by dynamic control of the specimen stage for atomic-resolution imaging
comment: 27 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to Ultramicroscopy Christophe Gatel: Writing original draft, Software, Methodology, Investigation, Data treatment, Conceptualization, Resources, Funding acquisition. Julien Dupuis: Software, Conceptualization, Methodology. Teresa Hungria: STEM experiment, Review & editing. Martin Hytch: Review & editing, Data treatment, Resources, Funding acquisition
summary: In this work, we show how the specimen drift can be actively compensated by controlling the stage with precision down to the picometre scale. We do this by dynamic control, a generic real-time feedback framework designed to actively stabilize electron microscopy experiments by continuously monitoring an experimental variable from the detector data stream and compensating its evolution during acquisition. The framework, applicable to a broad range of controllable experimental instabilities, includes automated calibration procedures, operates in parallel with image acquisition and is implemented as a software plugin without requiring any hardware modification of the microscope. Results for live drift correction are shown for a selection of TEM and STEM instruments using conventional mechanical stages as well as piezoelectric stages. Experimental results are presented for medium resolution TEM, high-resolution TEM, HR-STEM and in situ observations. With piezoelectric stages, specimen stabilization down to the picometre scale was achieved allowing drift-corrected atomic-resolution imaging. Specimen stage-based stabilization significantly improves long-exposure imaging and in situ experiments by increasing the effective exposure time, preserving the field of view, maintaining identical optical conditions and eliminating the need for numerical alignment of large datasets. Beyond the specific application presented here, dynamic control provides a versatile framework for real-time regulation of electron microscopy experiments and opens new perspectives for quantitative imaging, automated in situ studies and multimodal acquisitions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents dynamic control, a real-time feedback framework for actively compensating specimen drift in electron microscopy down to the picometre scale by controlling the microscope stage. Implemented as a software plugin requiring no hardware modification, it continuously monitors experimental variables from the detector data stream and compensates drift during acquisition. Results demonstrate picometre-scale stabilization across TEM and STEM instruments using both mechanical and piezoelectric stages, significantly improving long-exposure imaging and enabling drift-corrected atomic-resolution imaging.
AI.motivation: Specimen drift is a major limitation in electron microscopy, degrading long-exposure imaging, high-resolution imaging, and in situ experiments. Existing approaches typically rely on numerical post-processing alignment, which does not preserve the field of view or maintain identical optical conditions during acquisition, and they cannot correct drift in real time during the experiment.
AI.method: The authors implement dynamic control, a generic real-time feedback framework that monitors an experimental variable (specimen drift) from the detector data stream and compensates its evolution during acquisition by actively controlling the microscope stage. The framework includes automated calibration procedures, operates in parallel with image acquisition, and is deployed as a software plugin without hardware modifications to the microscope.
AI.result: Picometre-scale specimen stabilization was achieved with piezoelectric stages, enabling drift-corrected atomic-resolution imaging. Results are demonstrated across medium-resolution TEM, high-resolution TEM, HR-STEM, and in situ observations using both conventional mechanical stages and piezoelectric stages on various instruments.
AI.conclusion: Stage-based active drift compensation significantly improves long-exposure imaging and in situ experiments by increasing effective exposure time, preserving the field of view, maintaining identical optical conditions, and eliminating numerical alignment of large datasets. Dynamic control provides a versatile framework for real-time regulation of electron microscopy experiments, opening new avenues for quantitative imaging, automated in situ studies, and multimodal acquisitions.

title: A concentration-independent paradigm rendering weak interactions inherently quantifiable
comment: 95 pages, 6 figures, 19 supplementary figures. Companion paper submitted simultaneously: "Experimental access to molarity's blind spot in macroscopic assays" (F. Matsuda, M. Yoshimura, S. Ikeda, D. Fujita). Cross-references to the companion arXiv identifier will be added in v2
summary: A vast class of weak, millimolar-affinity molecular interactions governs cellular function, yet their quantitative characterization has remained largely beyond conventional methods. For over a century, biochemistry has worked within a concentration-based framework where molarity scales with molecular number per volume (N/V), and experiments have usually, often implicitly, changed concentration by moving N while holding V fixed. The weak-interaction measurement bottleneck arises from this paradigm: reading weak binding through bulk concentration requires concentrations beyond practical limits, a framework constraint rather than one of instrumental sensitivity. Here we show that shifting experimental control from N to accessible volume V overcomes this bottleneck and opens previously intractable affinity ranges through nanoscale spatial confinement. Controlling V means controlling what biochemists have called "local concentration" and "proximity effects," recasting these long-ambiguous notions as quantitative variables grounded in first principles. Implemented in DNA nanocavities, the approach showed that geometric arrangement alone can override solution-phase binding hierarchies. The same spatial control quantified a protein-peptide interaction of order 10 mM from femtomoles per well, totalling under a picomole per titration. Even so, a standard plate reader gave a signal-to-noise ratio near 10^3, leaving headroom for still weaker interactions. The affinity-and-geometry readout also enabled rational screening for protein-protein-interaction modulators, identifying compounds that enhance weak associations by reweighting local encounters rather than binding tightly on their own or forming a stable ternary complex. Together, this volume-based paradigm and its implementation provide a general strategy for probing and modulating previously inaccessible biochemical phenomena.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a volume-based paradigm for measuring weak, millimolar-affinity molecular interactions by shifting experimental control from molecular number (N) to accessible volume (V), employing nanoscale spatial confinement in DNA nanocavities. This approach bypasses the concentration limits that have historically prevented quantitative characterization of weak binding, achieving femtomole-level sensitivity and enabling rational screening of protein-protein interaction modulators.
AI.motivation: Weak, millimolar-affinity molecular interactions are ubiquitous in cellular function but have remained largely uncharacterizable by conventional biochemical methods. The bottleneck is not instrumental sensitivity but a paradigm constraint: reading weak binding through bulk concentration requires concentrations beyond practical limits. The authors aim to overcome this fundamental limitation by reevaluating how concentration is experimentally controlled.
AI.method: The authors shift experimental control from molecular number (N) to accessible volume (V), transforming concepts like "local concentration" and "proximity effects" into quantitatively defined, first-principles variables. Implemented in DNA nanocavities, the approach uses nanoscale spatial confinement to tune effective concentration, enabling affinity measurement and geometric control of binding hierarchies.
AI.result: Geometric arrangement alone could override solution-phase binding hierarchies. A protein-peptide interaction of ~10 mM affinity was quantified from femtomoles per well (under a picomole per titration total), yielding a signal-to-noise ratio near 10^3 on a standard plate reader. The affinity-and-geometry readout also enabled rational screening of PPI modulators, identifying compounds that enhance weak associations by reweighting local encounters rather than binding tightly or forming stable ternary complexes.
AI.conclusion: The volume-based paradigm provides a general strategy for probing and modulating previously inaccessible biochemical phenomena, potentially opening intractable affinity ranges and enabling new approaches to weak-interaction measurement and drug modulation.

title: Scale-covariant liquid in nonlocal high Tc strange metals
summary: Experiments in recent years on high $T_c$ superconductors find a puzzling nodal scale-covariant self-energy with an exponent varying continuously with doping. We propose a mechanism: nonlocality induced by poorly screened effective repulsions $V_α(r) \sim 1/r^α$, where a continuously doping-dependent exponent $1 \le α\le 3$ naturally interpolates between the Mott insulating and Fermi liquid limits. We develop a phenomenology of hydrodynamic screening, finding a scale-covariant quasiparticle decay rate $Γ(ω,T) \propto T^γ Φ(ω/T)$ in energy $ω$ and temperature $T$, with $γ= 2-\frac{1}α$ for nonlocal $ 1 < α< 2$. Our results naturally capture the optimally doped to overdoped regimes, whereas the underdoped regime is qualitatively distinct. In our theory, spectroscopy-fitted exponents directly probe the charged fluid's effective spatial nonlocality. Nonlocality shows that quantum criticality is not necessary to explain scale-covariant phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that puzzling scale-covariant self-energy observed in high-Tc superconductors originates from nonlocality induced by poorly screened repulsive interactions Vα(r) ~ 1/r^α, where a doping-dependent exponent 1 ≤ α ≤ 3 interpolates between Mott insulating and Fermi liquid limits. A hydrodynamic screening phenomenology yields a scale-covariant quasiparticle decay rate Γ(ω,T) ∝ T^γΦ(ω/T) with γ = 2 - 1/α for 1 < α < 2, naturally capturing optimally-to-overdoped regimes while the underdoped regime is qualitatively distinct.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments on high-Tc superconductors reveal a puzzling nodal scale-covariant self-energy with a continuously doping-dependent exponent. The authors aim to explain this phenomenon without invoking quantum criticality, proposing nonlocality from poorly screened effective repulsions as the underlying mechanism.
AI.method: The authors develop a phenomenology of hydrodynamic screening based on nonlocal repulsive interactions Vα(r) ~ 1/r^α. They derive a scale-covariant quasiparticle decay rate Γ(ω,T) ∝ T^γΦ(ω/T) with exponent γ = 2 - 1/α for nonlocal interactions in the regime 1 < α < 2, where α is a continuously doping-dependent parameter.
AI.result: The theory naturally captures the optimally doped to overdoped regimes, where the doping-dependent exponent γ interpolates between Mott insulating and Fermi liquid limits. The spectroscopy-fitted exponents directly probe the charged fluid's effective spatial nonlocality. The underdoped regime is shown to be qualitatively distinct.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocality arising from poorly screened repulsions can explain scale-covariant phenomena in high-Tc superconductors without invoking quantum criticality. Spectroscopic measurements of the exponent provide direct access to the effective spatial nonlocality of the charged fluid.

title: Discrepancy between the H-Function and Entropy: Insights into the rigorously established Boltzmann equation for hard-sphere gases
summary: By investigating the origin of the evolutionary discrepancy between the H-function and entropy, we elucidate that the H-function fails to serve as a valid arrow-of-time criterion in the rigorously derived Boltzmann equation for the hard-sphere gas model under the Boltzmann-Grad limit.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the H-function cannot serve as a valid arrow-of-time criterion in the rigorously derived Boltzmann equation for hard-sphere gases under the Boltzmann-Grad limit, due to discrepancies between the H-function and entropy.
AI.motivation: To explain why the H-function, traditionally used as an arrow-of-time indicator, fails to properly reflect thermodynamic entropy evolution in the rigorously derived Boltzmann equation framework.
AI.method: Investigating the origin of the evolutionary discrepancy between the H-function and entropy within the rigorously derived Boltzmann equation for the hard-sphere gas model under the Boltzmann-Grad limit.
AI.result: The H-function is demonstrated to be an invalid arrow-of-time criterion in the rigorously derived Boltzmann equation for the hard-sphere gas under the Boltzmann-Grad limit.
AI.conclusion: The H-function's inability to serve as a valid arrow-of-time criterion resolves the conceptual tension between the H-theorem and entropy production in the rigorous kinetic theory framework.

title: Hidden Quantum Geometry in Bilayer Exciton Condensates
comment: Maintext: 6 pages, 2 figures; Supplemental material: 5 pages
summary: When an electron-doped layer is stacked with a hole-doped layer with approximately equal carrier density, inter-layer Coulomb interaction turns the bilayer system into an exciton condensate (EC). In this Letter, we reveal a fundamental property of bilayer ECs: the excitonic order gives rise to nontrivial hidden quantum geometric effects in the correlated electron-hole bands, even when the non-interacting bands are trivial. Such peculiar EC-driven quantum geometry manifests itself in a characteristic out-of-plane polarization response upon applying an in-plane AC electric field to the bilayer EC system. In particular, the second-order response exhibits a characteristic inverse square scaling with the bilayer EC order parameter. Our finding reveals a fundamental hidden Berry phase effect driven by electron-hole correlations, and establishes bilayer EC as a promising platform for rich nonlinear physics.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that bilayer exciton condensates (ECs), formed by stacking electron-doped and hole-doped layers with equal carrier density, exhibit nontrivial hidden quantum geometric effects in correlated electron-hole bands even when non-interacting bands are trivial. This EC-driven quantum geometry manifests as a characteristic out-of-plane polarization response to in-plane AC electric fields, with the second-order response scaling inversely with the square of the EC order parameter, establishing bilayer ECs as a platform for nonlinear physics.
AI.motivation: To uncover fundamental properties of bilayer exciton condensates, specifically whether excitonic order can generate hidden quantum geometric effects (Berry phase-like) in correlated bands even when non-interacting bands are topologically trivial, and to demonstrate how these effects manifest in experimentally observable nonlinear responses.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze bilayer exciton condensate systems formed by electron-doped and hole-doped layers with nearly equal carrier densities, driven by inter-layer Coulomb interactions. They investigate how the excitonic order parameter generates quantum geometric effects in the correlated electron-hole bands and analyze the nonlinear optical response (second-order out-of-plane polarization) to in-plane AC electric fields.
AI.result: The excitonic order induces nontrivial hidden quantum geometric effects (Berry phase effects) in correlated electron-hole bands even when non-interacting bands are trivial. The second-order polarization response to an in-plane AC field exhibits a characteristic inverse square scaling with the EC order parameter.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a fundamental hidden Berry phase effect driven by electron-hole correlations and establish bilayer exciton condensates as a promising platform for rich nonlinear physics.

title: Apparent Dresselhaus coefficient in (001) GaAs quantum wells: Correlation-time renormalization in D'yakonov-Perel' spin relaxation
summary: We study the Dresselhaus coefficient inferred from D'yakonov-Perel' spin relaxation in bulk GaAs and (001) GaAs quantum wells using nonballistic Monte Carlo simulations. In bulk GaAs, inelastic LO-phonon simulations reproduce the spin relaxation with a cubic Dresselhaus coefficient γ_{3D}\simeq12.4 eVÅ^3 and a cubic-field correlation time τ_3^{3D}\simeq150 fs. In a projected two-dimensional quantum-well model, however, k_z^2 is replaced by the static expectation value \langle k_z^2 \rangle, converting the dominant Dresselhaus field into a term linear in the in-plane wave vector. We show that this projection changes the D'yakonov-Perel' correlation kernel from K_3^{2D} to a first- and third-order hybridized kernel K_{1+3}^{2D}, for which the correlation time τ_{1+3}^{2D} approaches 235 fs in the strict two-dimensional limit, in contrast to the third-order correlation time τ_3^{2D} of 130 fs. Consequently, the coefficient entering the projected two-dimensional model is not the intrinsic cubic coefficient itself but an apparent coefficient, γ_{2D}^{app}=γ_{3D} \sqrt{τ_3^{2D}/τ_{1+3}^{2D}}. Since τ_{1+3}^{2D}\simeq1.8τ_3^{2D} under LO-phonon-dominated scattering, γ_{2D}^{app}\simeq9.2 eVÅ^3, consistent with spin relaxation in (001) GaAs quantum wells. This correlation-time renormalization clarifies why Dresselhaus coefficients extracted from two-dimensional spin relaxation can differ from the cubic bulk coefficient and provides a useful framework for interpreting linear and cubic Dresselhaus parameters in quantum wells.

AI.tldr: The paper uses nonballistic Monte Carlo simulations to study Dresselhaus spin relaxation in bulk GaAs and (001) GaAs quantum wells. In bulk, spin relaxation is reproduced with a cubic Dresselhaus coefficient γ_{3D}≈12.4 eVÅ³ and correlation time τ_3^{3D}≈150 fs. In 2D quantum wells, the projection converts the Dresselhaus field into a hybridized linear-plus-cubic kernel K_{1+3}^{2D} with a longer correlation time (235 fs vs 130 fs), yielding an apparent coefficient γ_{2D}^{app}≈9.2 eVÅ³. This correlation-time renormalization explains why 2D-extracted Dresselhaus coefficients differ from the bulk cubic value.
AI.motivation: To clarify why Dresselhaus coefficients extracted from two-dimensional quantum-well spin relaxation differ from the intrinsic cubic bulk GaAs value, by examining how the k_z projection renormalizes the D'yakonov-Perel' correlation time and the apparent coupling coefficient.
AI.method: Nonballistic Monte Carlo simulations of D'yakonov-Perel' spin relaxation in bulk GaAs and (001) GaAs quantum wells, with LO-phonon-mediated inelastic scattering. The 2D projection replaces k_z² with ⟨k_z²⟩, converting the cubic Dresselhaus term into a linear-in-k_∥ term, and the D'yakonov-Perel' correlation kernel is analyzed from K_3^{2D} to a hybridized K_{1+3}^{2D}. Simulation-derived correlation times τ are used to define an apparent 2D coefficient γ_{2D}^{app}=γ_{3D}√(τ_3^{2D}/τ_{1+3}^{2D}).
AI.result: Bulk GaAs reproduces spin relaxation with γ_{3D}≈12.4 eVÅ³ and τ_3^{3D}≈150 fs. In the strict 2D limit, the hybridized kernel has correlation time τ_{1+3}^{2D}≈235 fs versus τ_3^{2D}≈130 fs for the pure cubic kernel, giving a renormalization factor of ~1.8 and an apparent coefficient γ_{2D}^{app}≈9.2 eVÅ³, consistent with spin relaxation in (001) quantum wells.
AI.conclusion: The projected 2D model does not measure the intrinsic cubic Dresselhaus coefficient directly; rather, correlation-time renormalization from the linear-plus-cubic hybridized D'yakonov-Perel' kernel produces an apparent coefficient lower than the bulk value. This provides a framework for correctly interpreting linear and cubic Dresselhaus parameters in quantum-well spin relaxation studies.

title: Fibonacci number systems and the localization criterion in the many-body Aubry-André model
summary: We introduce an extension of the Fibonacci number system, we call the fractional Fibonacci number system, which interpolates between the Fibonacci number system (used for natural numbers) and the irrational base-$φ$ number system, which can be used to represent real numbers. The number system finds its use in interpreting the localization phase diagram of the many-body non-interacting Aubry-André model. For finite system sizes a localization criterion can be obtained if the particle density is written in the fractional Fibonacci number system. In the thermodynamic limit, the criterion remains, but in this case the particle density is expressed in base-$φ$. The nature of the thermodynamic limit is also discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a "fractional Fibonacci number system" that interpolates between the standard Fibonacci number system (for natural numbers) and the irrational base-φ number system (for real numbers). This system is used to interpret the localization phase diagram of the many-body non-interacting Aubry-André model, providing a localization criterion for finite system sizes, which persists in the thermodynamic limit where the particle density is expressed in base-φ.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop a unified number system that bridges the Fibonacci number system and the base-φ number system, enabling a deeper interpretation of the localization phase diagram of the Aubry-André model across different system size regimes.
AI.method: The paper constructs a fractional Fibonacci number system that interpolates between integer Fibonacci representations and the base-φ representation. The particle density in the Aubry-André model is expressed in this new number system to derive a localization criterion for finite systems, and the criterion is examined in the thermodynamic limit where the density is given in base-φ.
AI.result: A localization criterion is obtained for finite system sizes by expressing the particle density in the fractional Fibonacci number system. In the thermodynamic limit, the same criterion holds but with the density expressed in base-φ. The nature of the thermodynamic limit is also discussed.
AI.conclusion: The fractional Fibonacci number system provides a useful framework for interpreting localization in the Aubry-André model, connecting finite-size behavior (Fibonacci-based) with the thermodynamic limit (base-φ-based).

title: Adaptive Inference and Convergence of Free Energy Landscapes Using Non-parametric Bayesian Enhanced Sampling
summary: Enhanced sampling techniques are central to the study of statistically rare events in the computer modeling and simulation of molecular phenomena. In this work, we report the development and integration of a Gaussian process model, adaptive, uncertainty-driven sampling scheme for enhanced sampling. The framework trains a Gaussian process model on an iteratively improving estimate of the free energy landscape. Regions of high uncertainty within the reaction phase space are increasingly sampled, and the uncertainty is computed on-the-fly during free energy reconstruction, serving as a convergence metric. This approach provides a generalizable strategy that can be extended to complex molecular processes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a novel enhanced sampling framework that uses a Gaussian process model with adaptive, uncertainty-driven sampling to iteratively estimate the free energy landscape for studying rare molecular events. High-uncertainty regions are preferentially sampled, with uncertainty serving as an on-the-fly convergence metric.
AI.motivation: Enhanced sampling is essential for studying statistically rare molecular events, but existing approaches often lack a generalizable, adaptive strategy for efficiently exploring reaction phase space and determining convergence.
AI.method: A Gaussian process model is trained on an iteratively improving estimate of the free energy landscape. Sampling is directed toward regions of high uncertainty in reaction phase space, with uncertainty computed on-the-fly during free energy reconstruction and used as a convergence metric.
AI.result: The framework provides a generalizable enhanced sampling strategy that can be extended to complex molecular processes, leveraging uncertainty-driven exploration for efficient free energy reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The uncertainty-aware Gaussian process approach offers a robust and adaptable enhanced sampling methodology with built-in convergence assessment, suitable for complex molecular systems.

title: Exotic superconductivity in the doped Kitaev quantum spin liquid
summary: We investigate superconductivity in a doped Kitaev quantum spin liquid by applying the many-variable variational Monte Carlo method to the hole-doped $t$-$J$-type Kitaev model. Using a projected pair-product wave function that can exactly represent the Kitaev quantum spin liquid, we examine the stability of superconducting phases on isotropic two-dimensional clusters. For the ferromagnetic Kitaev interaction, robust triplet $p$-wave superconductivity coexists with ferromagnetism in the low-to-intermediate doping regime but is suppressed as the system approaches the fully polarized ferromagnetic phase. For the antiferromagnetic Kitaev interaction, superconductivity exhibits a change in the dominant pairing symmetry from spin-dependent triplet $p$-wave at low doping to singlet $d+id$ at intermediate doping. By varying the strength of the ferromagnetic Kitaev interaction at fixed doping, we show that the triplet superconductivity increases together with the ferromagnetic moment and becomes strongest slightly below full polarization. Our results provide a theoretical basis for experimental searches for unconventional superconductivity, such as triplet superconductivity coexisting with ferromagnetism, in carrier-doped Kitaev candidate materials.

AI.tldr: The paper uses many-variable variational Monte Carlo to study superconductivity in a hole-doped Kitaev quantum spin liquid, finding robust triplet p-wave superconductivity coexisting with ferromagnetism for ferromagnetic Kitaev interactions, and a pairing symmetry crossover from triplet p-wave to singlet d+id for antiferromagnetic interactions as doping increases.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether unconventional superconductivity, particularly triplet superconductivity, can emerge in carrier-doped Kitaev quantum spin liquid materials, and to provide a theoretical foundation for experimental searches in Kitaev candidate compounds.
AI.method: Application of the many-variable variational Monte Carlo method to a hole-doped t-J-type Kitaev model, using a projected pair-product wave function that exactly represents the Kitaev quantum spin liquid, on isotropic two-dimensional clusters.
AI.result: For ferromagnetic Kitaev interaction, robust triplet p-wave superconductivity coexists with ferromagnetism at low-to-intermediate doping but is suppressed near full polarization. For antiferromagnetic Kitaev interaction, dominant pairing symmetry changes from spin-dependent triplet p-wave at low doping to singlet d+id at intermediate doping. Triplet superconductivity increases with ferromagnetic moment and peaks slightly below full polarization.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a theoretical basis for experimental searches for unconventional superconductivity, such as triplet superconductivity coexisting with ferromagnetism, in carrier-doped Kitaev candidate materials.

title: The intermediate scattering function of an interacting adlayer as a characteristic function: a closed-form theory of Ising lattice-gas surface diffusion
summary: The intermediate scattering function (ISF) measured by helium spin-echo is a characteristic function (CF): the Fourier transform of the distribution of adsorbate displacements, whose value at zero time is the static structure factor.
