We use this double role to bring lateral interactions of Ising lattice-gas type into surface diffusion. The ISF then follows in closed form in momentum transfer, time, coverage and temperature, and with it the whole linear-response hierarchy. A single correlation parameter fixes both the equilibrium structure and the interaction-renormalized hop rate; it is exact along a one-dimensional channel, and is carried onto the surface as the nearest-neighbour correlation of a pair approximation, the momentum dependence of the structure factor then coming from a collective (random-phase) treatment. The closed form is not postulated. Projecting the master equation onto the density gives an exact equation of motion whose amplitude is an identity and whose initial rate obeys a sum rule, so that the quasi-elastic weight is the layer's own structure factor and de Gennes narrowing becomes a theorem rather than an analogy; the closed form is what remains when the memory kernel of that equation is dropped. Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) on the same Hamiltonian reproduces the dressed hop rate to better than about one per cent and the initial collective rate to $1$--$2\%$. Four correlated, non-critical fingerprints of the interaction follow --- in the quasi-elastic amplitude, its linewidth, the Arrhenius slope, and the dependence of the fitted linewidth on the range of times over which the decay is fitted. They invert in closed form for the attempt frequency, the static barrier and the interaction. Applications to Na/Cu(111) and H/Pt(111) are analysed and discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a closed-form analytical expression for the intermediate scattering function (ISF) measured by helium spin-echo for surface diffusion with Ising lattice-gas lateral interactions. The ISF, which is the Fourier transform of the displacement distribution, is expressed exactly along 1D channels and approximately on surfaces via a pair-approximation nearest-neighbour correlation and random-phase (collective) structure factor. The closed form, obtained by projecting the master equation onto the density and dropping the memory kernel, reproduces KMC simulations to within ~1-2%, and yields four non-critical fingerprints of lateral interactions that invert in closed form for the attempt frequency, static barrier, and interaction energy.
AI.motivation: To bring lateral interactions of Ising lattice-gas type into the analysis of surface diffusion measured by helium spin-echo spectroscopy, since interacting adsorbates introduce non-trivial collective effects not captured by non-interacting theories.
AI.method: The authors exploit the double role of the ISF as a characteristic function (whose zero-time value is the static structure factor). They project the master equation onto the density to obtain an exact equation of motion, whose memory kernel is dropped to yield a closed-form ISF. A single correlation parameter fixes both equilibrium structure and interaction-renormalized hop rate, using exact nearest-neighbour correlation in 1D and a pair approximation with random-phase treatment for surfaces. Validation is performed with Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.

Four correlated, non-critical fingerprints of interaction are identified (quasi-elastic amplitude, linewidth, Arrhenius slope, and fitted-linewidth dependence on fit-time range), all invertible in closed form for the attempt frequency, static barrier, and interaction. Applications to Na/Cu(111) and H/Pt(111) are analysed.
AI.conclusion: The closed-form ISF, derived from first principles rather than postulated, provides a rigorous framework for extracting lateral interaction parameters from helium spin-echo data, with de Gennes narrowing emerging as a theorem from the sum rule rather than an analogy, and enables direct inversion of experimental fingerprints into microscopic kinetic parameters.

title: Quaternion-Kahler geometry of time reversal symmetric crystals
summary: Quantum geometry reveals how the shape of Bloch wave functions governs correlated quantum phenomena. Its standard formulation describes isolated complex bands, where Berry curvature is Abelian and ideal geometry is Kahler. However, time reversal symmetric crystals with spin require a different language since Kramers degeneracy pairs Bloch states and turns Berry curvature into a non-Abelian SU(2) field. Here we show that Kramers pair band geometry is quaternionic. A minimal Kramers pair defines a map into quaternion projective space, and its quaternionic quantum geometric tensor unifies the quantum metric with the three SU(2) Berry curvature components. The non-negativity of this tensor imposes local metric-curvature inequalities, whose saturation defines the non-Abelian counterpart of ideal Chern bands. In four dimensions, the ideal limit further yields an algebraic structure related to the four-dimensional quantum Hall effect. Our results promote ideal quantum geometry from the Abelian geometry of Chern bands to the quaternionic, non-Abelian geometry of time reversal symmetric quantum matter.

AI.tldr: This paper extends quantum geometry from Abelian (complex) to non-Abelian quaternionic geometry for Kramers-paired bands in time-reversal symmetric crystals, introducing a quaternionic quantum geometric tensor that unifies the quantum metric with three SU(2) Berry curvature components and establishing local metric-curvature inequalities whose saturation defines ideal non-Abelian bands.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum geometry describes isolated complex bands with Abelian Berry curvature and Kähler ideal geometry, but time-reversal symmetric crystals with spin require a different formulation because Kramers degeneracy pairs Bloch states and promotes Berry curvature to a non-Abelian SU(2) field. A new language is needed to capture the geometry of such systems.
AI.method: The authors show that Kramers pair band geometry is quaternionic. A minimal Kramers pair defines a map into quaternion projective space, and its quaternionic quantum geometric tensor unifies the quantum metric with the three SU(2) Berry curvature components. The non-negativity of this tensor imposes local metric-curvature inequalities, with saturation defining the non-Abelian analogue of ideal Chern bands.
AI.result: The quaternionic quantum geometric tensor provides a unified description of metric and curvature for Kramers pairs. Non-negativity yields local inequalities between metric and SU(2) curvature. In four dimensions, the saturated ideal limit gives an algebraic structure related to the four-dimensional quantum Hall effect.
AI.conclusion: Ideal quantum geometry is promoted from Abelian geometry of Chern bands to quaternionic, non-Abelian geometry of time-reversal symmetric quantum matter, providing a generalized framework for correlated quantum phenomena involving spin.

title: Resolving Peak Shifting Effects in Real-Time Time-Dependent Orbital Propagation Methods Through Nonorthogonal Expansions
summary: Self-consistent field real-time electronic structure methods are a powerful approach for modeling ultrafast processes but suffer from systematic errors in predicted transition energies, commonly known as peak shifting, that obscure direct comparison with experiment. Although this effect has been explored in single reference methods, a general understanding that extends to multiconfigurational methods remains unresolved. Here, we develop a real-time nonorthogonal multiconfigurational self-consistent field (RT-TD NOMCSCF) formalism in which independently propagated orbital sets generate a compact, nonorthogonal wavefunction. The approach establishes a unified framework for nonlinear real-time electronic structure theories, which we use to reveal the common origin of peak shifting across single and multireference limits. Using this framework, we demonstrate that peak shifting does not arise exclusively from the effect of state averaging over the internal space basis, but also from the accessible external configurational space. By systematically expanding the internal space with independently propagated orbital sets, RT-TD NOMCSCF suppresses this aver- aging, recovers correct transition energies, and distinguishes intrinsic peak shifting from numerical peak drifting caused by propagation errors. Thus, these developments establish nonlinear real-time electronic structure methods that enables more accurate simulations of ultrafast processes.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a real-time nonorthogonal multiconfigurational self-consistent field (RT-TD NOMCSCF) formalism that identifies the common origin of peak shifting in nonlinear real-time electronic structure methods across single- and multireference limits, and shows that peak shifting arises not only from state averaging over the internal space but also from the accessible external configurational space.
AI.motivation: Real-time electronic structure methods suffer from systematic errors in predicted transition energies (peak shifting) that obscure comparison with experiment. While this effect has been studied in single-reference methods, a general understanding extending to multiconfigurational methods has remained unresolved.
AI.method: The authors develop RT-TD NOMCSCF, a real-time nonorthogonal multiconfigurational self-consistent field formalism where independently propagated orbital sets generate a compact nonorthogonal wavefunction. This establishes a unified framework for nonlinear real-time electronic structure theories that connects single- and multireference limits. The internal space is systematically expanded with independently propagated orbital sets.

RT-TD NOMCSCF suppresses state averaging by expanding the internal space, recovers correct transition energies, and distinguishes intrinsic peak shifting from numerical peak drifting caused by propagation errors.

title: Surface-Selective Probe of Spin-Triplet Superconductivity in Rhombohedral Graphene
summary: Superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene has been observed across many layer numbers, with mounting evidence pointing toward spin-triplet pairing, yet complementary probes of the superconducting spin structure remain needed. Here we use one-sided WS$_2$ proximity in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene (R5G) as a surface-selective spin-orbit probe. The induced Ising spin-orbit coupling is strongest for carriers localized near the WS$_2$ interface, allowing the displacement field to tune the overlap between superconducting carriers and the spin-orbit perturbation. We observe a strongly asymmetric superconducting landscape: two robust pockets, SC1 and SC2, survive only on mutually opposite signs of displacement field, while a third pocket, SC3, is substantially weaker. Gate-tracking features, quantum oscillations, and self-consistent band-structure calculations identify the layer polarization and Fermi-surface character of the relevant carriers. The robust superconducting states are absent or strongly weakened when the active high-DOS carriers are polarized toward the WS$_2$ interface. Since Ising spin-orbit coupling is compatible with time-reversed spin-singlet pairing but competes with same-spin intervalley triplet pairing by canting or pinning the parent spin texture, this surface-selective suppression provides additional evidence for spin-triplet superconductivity involving both hole-like and electron-like carriers. Our results establish one-sided TMD proximity as a displacement-field-tunable probe of superconducting spin structure in rhombohedral graphene.

AI.tldr: The authors use one-sided WS₂ proximity in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene (R5G) as a surface-selective spin-orbit probe to investigate the superconducting spin structure. They observe a strongly asymmetric superconducting landscape where robust superconducting pockets survive only for specific displacement-field polarities, and show that superconductivity is suppressed or weakened when the active high-density-of-states carriers are polarized toward the WS₂ interface. Since Ising spin-orbit coupling is compatible with spin-singlet pairing but competes with same-spin intervalley triplet pairing, this surface-selective suppression provides evidence for spin-triplet superconductivity in R5G.
AI.motivation: Rhombohedral graphene superconductivity has been observed across many layer numbers with evidence pointing toward spin-triplet pairing, yet complementary probes of the superconducting spin structure remain needed. A surface-selective, displacement-field-tunable probe is required to directly interrogate the spin character of the superconducting state.

The Ising spin-orbit coupling induced by WS₂ is strongest near the interface, so the displacement field tunes the overlap between superconducting carriers and the spin-orbit perturbation. They combine gate-tracking features, quantum oscillations, and self-consistent band-structure calculations to identify layer polarization and Fermi-surface character.
AI.result: Three superconducting pockets (SC1, SC2, SC3) are observed with strongly asymmetric behavior: SC1 and SC2 survive only on mutually opposite displacement-field signs, while SC3 is substantially weaker. Robust superconducting states are absent or strongly weakened when the active high-DOS carriers are polarized toward the WS₂ interface.
AI.conclusion: The surface-selective suppression of superconductivity when carriers overlap the Ising spin-orbit perturbation is interpreted as evidence for spin-triplet pairing. Since Ising SOC is compatible with spin-singlet pairing but competes with same-spin intervalley triplet pairing, the observed suppression supports spin-triplet superconductivity involving both hole-like and electron-like carriers. This establishes one-sided TMD proximity as a displacement-field-tunable probe of superconducting spin structure in rhombohedral graphene.

title: Contrasting anisotropic electron-phonon-spin coupling in Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ and Fe$_{5}$GeTe$_{2}$: A helicity-resolved Raman study
comment: Main text: 15 pages, 8 figures + Supplemental Material: 6 pages, 5 figures
summary: Two-dimensional van der Waals ferromagnets Fe$_3$GeTe$ _2$ (F3GT) and Fe$_5$GeTe$_2$ (F5GT) exhibit pronounced magneto-optical responses, which open promising platforms for investigating the interplay among lattice, electronic, and magnetic degrees of freedom. Here, we present a comparative study of optical resonance-induced anisotropic electron-phonon coupling and its association with magnetic ordering in these systems using wavelength- and temperature-dependent helicity-resolved Raman spectroscopy. By resolving the doubly degenerate E modes under left- and right-circularly polarized excitations, we demonstrate that the temperature evolution of the chiral mode splitting ($Δf$) does not track the magnetization behavior, indicating that the helicity-dependent Raman response arises not solely from time-reversal symmetry breaking due to magnetic order, but also from spin-orbit-coupled electronic interactions. Notably, in F3GT, the out-of-plane magnetization indirectly governs the in-plane anisotropic electron-phonon coupling under optical resonance, whereas F5GT exhibits static anisotropic interactions. The Fano asymmetry parameter $1/q$ reveals mode- and temperature-dependent coupling strengths between phonons and the electronic continuum, with pronounced angular anisotropy in F3GT but isotropic behavior in F5GT--- a consequence of its multiple Fe sites and enhanced interlayer hybridization in the latter. Our results demonstrate the role of crystal structure and magnetic anisotropy in shaping the anisotropically coupled electron-phonon-spin dynamics in these layered metallic ferromagnets, and highlight Fe$_x$GeTe$_2$ as a versatile platform for microscopic insight into chiral light-matter interactions in layered metallic ferromagnets.

The study further demonstrates that crystal structure and magnetic anisotropy shape anisotropic electron-phonon-spin coupling, with distinct behaviors between the two materials.

title: Helicity in monoaxial chiral magnets
summary: The equilibrium state of a monoaxial chiral magnet surrounded by a non-magnetic medium (such as air or vacuum) is a helical texture characterized by a single, well-defined wave vector. No metastable states have ever been observed in such systems. Recently, however, it was demonstrated that when a chiral magnet is in close contact with two uniaxial ferromagnets, a large number of metastable helical states emerge in addition to the equilibrium state [Phys. Rev. B 109, 214424]. These helical states are distinguished by their wave number (helicity). In the present work, we elucidate the topological origin of the stabilization of these states --a mechanism we term dynamical topological protection-- and investigate their static and dynamic properties. We find that, as a consequence of this dynamical topological protection, the winding number of the helical states remains constant under the application of sufficiently weak magnetic fields and polarized electric currents. Furthermore, when a polarized current is applied to a metastable helical state, a static configuration is reached. This state retains the original winding number, but its winding number density becomes non-homogeneously distributed, concentrating near the interface with one of the ferromagnets. The dynamic response to sufficiently large magnetic fields and currents provides mechanisms to switch between different helical states. Since the magnetic properties depend on helicity, these metastable helical states are highly promising for applications in spintronics and magnonics.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals the topological origin (termed "dynamical topological protection") behind the stabilization of metastable helical states in monoaxial chiral magnets coupled to two uniaxial ferromagnets, and investigates their static and dynamic properties, including stability under magnetic fields and currents, current-driven winding-number-preserving relaxation, and field/current-driven switching between helical states with potential spintronics and magnonics applications.
AI.motivation: In pristine monoaxial chiral magnets surrounded by non-magnetic media, only a single equilibrium helical state exists with no metastable states. However, recent work showed that contacting a chiral magnet with two uniaxial ferromagnets generates numerous metastable helical states distinguished by their helicity (wave number). The present work aims to explain the topological origin of this stabilization and to characterize the static and dynamic behavior of these states.
AI.method: The authors develop a topological framework to explain the stabilization of metastable helical states, introducing the concept of "dynamical topological protection." They analyze the static and dynamic properties of these states analytically and/or numerically, examining their behavior under weak magnetic fields, polarized electric currents, and strong perturbations to understand both stability and switching mechanisms.
AI.result: (1) The winding number of helical states remains invariant under sufficiently weak magnetic fields and polarized electric currents due to dynamical topological protection. (2) Under a polarized current, a metastable helical state relaxes to a static configuration preserving the original winding number, but with non-homogeneously distributed winding-number density concentrated near one ferromagnet interface. (3) Large magnetic fields and currents can switch between different helical states, providing a control mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The metastable helical states in ferromagnet-coupled chiral magnets are topologically protected dynamically and their magnetic properties depend on helicity. This makes them highly promising for spintronics and magnonics applications, where controlled switching and stable distinct states are required.

title: Bias Tunable Transport Modulation and Gas Selectivity in Layered BiOI: A DFT NEGF Study
summary: Understanding the interplay between adsorption energetics and charge-transport modulation is essential for the rational design of low-power and bias-tunable gas sensors. Here, we present a comprehensive first-principles study of gas selectivity in layered bismuth oxyiodide (BiOI) by integrating density functional theory with nonequilibrium Green's function transport calculations. The adsorption and bias-dependent transport responses toward NO2, NH3, CO2, and representative volatile organic compounds are systematically examined. While NH3 and NO2 exhibit strong chemisorption and localized electronic perturbations, CO2 interacts through weak physisorption, demonstrating that adsorption strength alone does not determine sensing performance. Instead, the evolution of transmission channels near the Fermi level governs the sensing response. Bias-dependent calculations reveal an electrically tunable sensitivity hierarchy, in which weakly adsorbed CO2 preserves conductive pathways and exhibits pronounced low-bias sensitivity despite minimal charge transfer. Recovery-time analysis further highlights the trade-off between transport modulation and reversibility for strongly adsorbed species. These results establish a transport-centered selectivity framework for layered BiOI and provide mechanistic insight into electric-field-controlled gas sensing under ambient conditions.

AI.tldr: A first-principles study combining DFT with nonequilibrium Green's function transport calculations demonstrates that gas sensing selectivity in layered BiOI is governed by transmission channel evolution near the Fermi level rather than adsorption strength alone, with weakly adsorbed CO2 showing pronounced low-bias sensitivity.
AI.motivation: To understand how adsorption energetics and charge-transport modulation interplay in gas sensors, enabling rational design of low-power and bias-tunable sensing devices.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) integrated with nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) transport calculations to systematically examine bias-dependent adsorption and transport responses of BiOI toward NO2, NH3, CO2, and volatile organic compounds.
AI.result: NH3 and NO2 show strong chemisorption with localized electronic perturbations while CO2 exhibits weak physisorption; adsorption strength alone does not determine sensing performance—transmission channel evolution near the Fermi level governs response. Bias-dependent calculations reveal electrically tunable sensitivity where weakly adsorbed CO2 preserves conductive pathways and shows high low-bias sensitivity despite minimal charge transfer; recovery-time analysis highlights a trade-off between transport modulation and reversibility for strongly adsorbed species.
AI.conclusion: A transport-centered selectivity framework is established for layered BiOI, providing mechanistic insight into electric-field-controlled gas sensing under ambient conditions.

title: Cooling down trees for finite-temperature quantum dynamics: Purification within ML-MCTDH
summary: Simulating multidimensional quantum systems at finite temperature is inherently challenging as the system is no longer described by a single, pure-state wavefunction but by a density operator, squaring an already exponential scaling of the Hilbert space. Building upon the compact wavefunction ansatz of the multi-layer multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree (ML-MCTDH) method, we present a new scheme for simulating finite-temperature quantum dynamics based on purification. Here, a density operator is mapped to a single ML-MCTDH wavefunction in an enlarged Hilbert space, comprising physical and auxiliary degrees of freedom. In the key step, one obtains a pure-state representation of the canonical density operator via imaginary time-propagation of the infinite-temperature state. The most important observation is that this state can be exactly decomposed as a Hartree product of maximally entangled combined modes, each combined mode consisting of a physical degree of freedom and its auxiliary counterpart. Through dynamically pruning the node ranks of the ML-tree during the "cool down" stage yields a compact finite-temperature wavefunction, thus accelerating the real-time propagation and enabling finite-temperature simulations of multidimensional, correlated molecular systems. Our method circumvents both intensive statistical sampling and costly tensor-decomposition of the full density-operator, while being broadly applicable to model Hamiltonians and general ab initio potential energy surfaces alike. Two applications of the method are presented, benchmark results on the thermal ground-state of H2O as well as temperature-dependent infrared absorption spectra of the more challenging, floppy H3O2- anion.

AI.motivation: Simulating multidimensional quantum systems at finite temperature is challenging because the system is described by a density operator rather than a pure-state wavefunction, which squares the already exponential scaling of the Hilbert space.
AI.method: The method maps a density operator to a single ML-MCTDH wavefunction in an enlarged Hilbert space with physical and auxiliary degrees of freedom. The canonical density operator is represented as a pure state via imaginary-time propagation of the infinite-temperature state, which can be exactly decomposed as a Hartree product of maximally entangled combined modes. Dynamically pruning the node ranks of the ML-tree during the cooling stage yields a compact finite-temperature wavefunction.

AI.conclusion: The method circumvents both intensive statistical sampling and costly tensor-decomposition of the full density operator, while being broadly applicable to model Hamiltonians and general ab initio potential energy surfaces alike.

title: Fluctuations of topological charges in two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model through high-temperature and low-temperature expansions
summary: It is well known that KT transition in 2d XY model is driven by the binding and unbinding of topological defects, which can be characterized by the fluctuation of topological charges inside a region. We extend the idea into the 2d Heisenberg model and calculate the fluctuation through high-temperature and low-temperature expansion respectively. It is found that the fluctuation of topological charges is proportional to the area of the region at high temperatures while obeys the perimeter law at low temperatures.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the concept of topological defect fluctuation (characteristic of the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in 2D XY model) to the 2D Heisenberg model, showing via high- and low-temperature expansions that topological charge fluctuation follows an area law at high temperatures and a perimeter law at low temperatures.
AI.motivation: The KT transition in the 2D XY model is driven by the binding/unbinding of topological defects, characterized by topological charge fluctuations inside a region. The authors aim to extend this topological characterization approach to the 2D Heisenberg model.
AI.method: The authors calculate the fluctuation of topological charges in the 2D Heisenberg model using high-temperature expansion and low-temperature expansion, respectively.
AI.result: Topological charge fluctuation is proportional to the area of the region at high temperatures, while it obeys a perimeter law at low temperatures.
AI.conclusion: The area-law vs. perimeter-law behavior of topological charge fluctuations distinguishes high- and low-temperature phases in the 2D Heisenberg model, analogous to the KT transition characterization in the 2D XY model.

title: Lower bounds on entropy production from dynamical correlation functions
summary: Entropy production is a key property in stochastic thermodynamics. For partially observed and coarse-grained systems, its inference is challenging and typically rests on proven lower bounds. We derive two versions of such bounds based on the asymmetry of experimentally accessible two-time correlation functions of coarse-grained state observables. For non-equilibrium steady states, the bound is valid for arbitrary correlation lag. For time-dependent processes, it requires the limit of vanishing lag. These bounds hold true for any system that follows either a Markovian dynamics or a coupled set of overdamped Langevin equations on some underlying, unobservable level of description. We illustrate the bounds for both types of dynamics and discuss their optimization and potential tightness.

AI.tldr: This paper derives two lower bounds on entropy production rate for partially observed or coarse-grained stochastic systems. The bounds are based on the asymmetry of two-time correlation functions of coarse-grained observable state variables, valid for non-equilibrium steady states (at any lag) and time-dependent processes (in the vanishing lag limit). They apply to systems with underlying Markovian dynamics or coupled overdamped Langevin equations.
AI.motivation: Entropy production is central to stochastic thermodynamics, but for experimentally accessible coarse-grained or partially observed systems, direct inference is challenging. The authors aim to derive provable lower bounds on entropy production that can be computed from experimentally accessible two-time correlation functions of observable variables.
AI.method: The authors derive two versions of entropy production bounds based on the asymmetry of two-time correlation functions of coarse-grained observables. The first bound applies to non-equilibrium steady states and is valid for arbitrary correlation lag; the second applies to time-dependent (non-stationary) processes and requires the limit of vanishing lag. The results hold for any system governed by either Markovian dynamics or coupled overdamped Langevin equations on an underlying hidden level of description.
AI.result: The derived bounds are valid for both Markovian dynamics and coupled overdamped Langevin equations and are illustrated for both dynamical types. The authors also discuss optimization strategies and potential tightness of the bounds.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides experimentally accessible lower bounds on entropy production based on correlation function asymmetries, applicable to a broad class of stochastic systems under coarse-graining, with discussion of optimization and tightness giving practical guidance for their usage.

title: Vector-field control and emergent basal-plane anisotropy of magnetic textures in noncentrosymmetric (Fe$_{0.63}$Ni$_{0.3}$Pd$_{0.07}$)$_3$P
summary: (Fe$_{0.63}$Ni$_{0.3}$Pd$_{0.07}$)$_3$P is a room-temperature magnet with $S_4$ symmetry that hosts a rich variety of topological spin textures. Here, we report a combined resonant small-angle x-ray scattering and ptychography study of (Fe$_{0.63}$Ni$_{0.3}$Pd$_{0.07}$)$_3$P in vector magnetic fields over a broad temperature range. We demonstrate deterministic vector-field control of magnetic stripe domains, where in-plane fields continuously rotate their orientation via a transition from a chiral stripe to an achiral fan configuration. Furthermore, at 50 K and below, the stripe orientation becomes metastably pinned and retains its field-trained direction. While the magnitude of the wavevector is nearly isotropic within the basal plane at room temperature, a pronounced temperature evolution of anisotropic interactions emerges upon cooling. In particular, non-trivial anisotropy axes develop at 20-50 K reflecting the combined effects of magnetocrystalline anisotropy, anisotropic exchange, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI), whose effective orientation is found to rotate with temperature. These results establish (Fe$_{0.63}$Ni$_{0.3}$Pd$_{0.07}$)$_3$P as a model system for vector-field control of chiral spin textures and reveal a previously unrecognized temperature-driven evolution of the effective DMI landscape in a noncentrosymmetric magnet.

AI.tldr: A combined resonant small-angle X-ray scattering and ptychography study of the room-temperature magnet (Fe₀.₆₃Ni₀.₃Pd₀.₀₇)₃P reveals deterministic vector-field control of magnetic stripe domains, metastable pinning of stripe orientation at low temperatures, and a temperature-driven evolution of anisotropic interactions including a rotating effective Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction landscape.
AI.motivation: To understand and demonstrate deterministic control of topological spin textures via vector magnetic fields in a noncentrosymmetric room-temperature magnet, and to uncover how temperature drives the evolution of anisotropic magnetic interactions (magnetocrystalline anisotropy, anisotropic exchange, and DMI).
AI.method: Combined resonant small-angle X-ray scattering (RSAXS) and X-ray ptychography measurements on (Fe₀.₆₃Ni₀.₃Pd₀.₀₇)₃P under vector magnetic fields across a broad temperature range.
AI.result: Vector-field control of magnetic stripe domains is demonstrated, with in-plane fields inducing a continuous rotation of stripe orientation via a chiral-to-achiral (fan) transition. Below 50 K, stripe orientation becomes metastably pinned. The wavevector is nearly isotropic at room temperature but develops pronounced anisotropic interactions upon cooling, with nontrivial anisotropy axes emerging at 20-50 K and the effective DMI orientation rotating with temperature.
AI.conclusion: (Fe₀.₆₃Ni₀.₃Pd₀.₀₇)₃P serves as a model system for vector-field control of chiral spin textures, and the study reveals a previously unrecognized temperature-driven evolution of the effective DMI landscape in noncentrosymmetric magnets.

title: Negative Differential Capacitance from Composition-Dependent Stern Capacitance in a Binary Mixture
summary: We develop a thermodynamic theory of electric double layers in binary liquid mixtures by allowing the Stern-layer capacitance to depend on the local solvent composition. This coupling produces an additional negative contribution to the inverse differential capacitance. As a result, the surface potential can become a nonmonotonic function of the surface charge density, leading to negative differential capacitance and a voltage-induced first-order transition between two electric-double-layer states. We determine the coexistence condition using a common-tangent construction for the surface-charge-controlled grand potential and obtain phase diagrams in terms of the Stern-capacitance contrast, surface charge density, bulk composition, and surface potential. We also compare the theory with capacitance data for tetrabutylammonium chloride in water/1-propanol mixtures, finding semi-quantitative agreement in the continuous-response regime. These results suggest that solvent exchange inside the Stern layer can strongly control the capacitance and interfacial phase behavior of binary mixtures.

AI.tldr: A thermodynamic theory of electric double layers in binary liquid mixtures is developed where the Stern-layer capacitance depends on local solvent composition, producing negative differential capacitance and a voltage-induced first-order transition between two EDL states. The theory shows semi-quantitative agreement with capacitance data for tetrabutylammonium chloride in water/1-propanol mixtures.
AI.motivation: To understand how solvent composition inside the Stern layer influences the capacitance and interfacial phase behavior of electric double layers in binary liquid mixtures, a coupling that has not been captured by existing models.
AI.method: The authors extend thermodynamic EDL theory by allowing the Stern-layer capacitance to depend on the local solvent composition. A common-tangent construction is used on the surface-charge-controlled grand potential to determine coexistence conditions between two EDL states, and phase diagrams are constructed in terms of Stern-capacitance contrast, surface charge density, bulk composition, and surface potential.
AI.result: The composition-dependent Stern capacitance produces an additional negative contribution to the inverse differential capacitance, leading to nonmonotonic surface potential versus surface charge, negative differential capacitance, and a first-order transition between EDL states. The theory achieves semi-quantitative agreement with experimental capacitance data for tetrabutylammonium chloride in water/1-propanol mixtures in the continuous-response regime.
AI.conclusion: Solvent exchange inside the Stern layer can strongly control the capacitance and interfacial phase behavior of binary liquid mixtures, offering a framework to predict and interpret composition-dependent EDL phenomena.

title: Magnetoresistance in Magnetic Weyl semimetal Mn$_{3}$ZnC
summary: The magnetoresistance (MR) in magnetic materials reveal an intriguing spin-dependent electron scattering, highlighting the role of spin polarization on the electronic transport properties. This becomes even more interesting for the topological magnetic materials where a finite Berry curvature leads to an intrinsic scattering channel also. In this report, we investigate MR of Mn$_{3}$ZnC, an antiperovskite magnetic nodal line semimetal. Mn$_{3}$ZnC shows a ferromagnetic (FM) transition at $\sim$ 420 K, followed by an ferrimagnetic (FIM) transition at $\sim$ 195 K. We focus on the interpretation of MR data and highlight the relation between MR and its magnetization. The signature of magnetization induced MR shows correlation at low magnetic fields and displays distinct behaviors in the FIM and FM states. Similar to the isothermal magnetization M(H) curve of FM and FIM state, the MR curves exhibit a sharp increase, followed by a linear behavior at higher fields. As the magnetic field varies, the cusp-like anomaly becomes more pronounced, and vanishes at the magnetic phase transition, which then reappears as the temperature increases. The sign change in the MR curves in the FIM state is attributed to a drastic change in the carrier mobility. Interestingly, this system shows a positive MR in FM state at very low field, which is quite unusual.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates magnetoresistance (MR) in Mn₃ZnC, an antiperovskite magnetic nodal line semimetal, revealing spin-dependent electron scattering and Berry curvature effects. The MR shows distinct behaviors in ferromagnetic (FM, below ~420 K) and ferrimagnetic (FIM, below ~195 K) states, with cusp-like anomalies at magnetic transitions, sign changes in FIM state due to carrier mobility changes, and an unusual positive MR in FM state at very low fields.
AI.motivation: To understand the spin-dependent electron scattering and intrinsic scattering channels (from Berry curvature) in topological magnetic materials, and to clarify the relationship between MR and magnetization in the antiperovskite magnetic nodal line semimetal Mn₃ZnC.
AI.method: Magnetoresistance measurements are carried out on Mn₃ZnC across its magnetic phase transitions (FM at ~420 K and FIM at ~195 K). The MR data is interpreted in relation to isothermal magnetization M(H) curves, analyzing field and temperature dependence of MR in both FM and FIM states.
AI.result: MR curves show a sharp increase followed by linear behavior at higher fields, mirroring the M(H) curves in both FM and FIM states. A cusp-like anomaly sharpens with varying field and disappears at the magnetic phase transition. A sign change in MR in the FIM state is attributed to drastic carrier mobility changes. Unusually, positive MR is observed in the FM state at very low fields.
AI.conclusion: The MR in Mn₃ZnC is strongly correlated with its magnetization, showing distinct field- and temperature-dependent signatures in FM and FIM states. The unusual positive low-field MR in the FM state and the mobility-driven MR sign change in the FIM state highlight the complex interplay between magnetic ordering, Berry curvature, and electronic transport in this topological magnetic material.

title: Kappa distributions as asymptotic marginals of exponential family ensembles
summary: Recently (Physica A 660 130370, 2025), emergence of superstatistical behavior in driven classical systems has been shown for systems with constant microcanonical heat capacity. As an application of this result, in this work we show that a system of $N$ particles with inverse gamma distribution of total kinetic energies must have kappa-distributed single-particle velocities in the limit $N \rightarrow \infty$. Our results provide insight into the nature of kappa distributions outside the theory of nonextensive statistical mechanics, while also bringing forward a practical method for the generation of kappa velocities via Monte Carlo Metropolis simulation in the inverse gamma ensemble.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that a system of N particles with inverse gamma-distributed total kinetic energies produces kappa-distributed single-particle velocities in the thermodynamic limit (N→∞), building on recent superstatistical results for driven classical systems. It offers a practical Monte Carlo Metropolis method for generating kappa velocities in the inverse gamma ensemble.
AI.motivation: To provide insight into the nature of kappa distributions outside the framework of nonextensive statistical mechanics, and to offer an alternative derivation of kappa-distributed velocities from an inverse gamma ensemble.
AI.method: The work applies recent results on superstatistical behavior in driven classical systems (for systems with constant microcanonical heat capacity) to show that inverse gamma-distributed total kinetic energies over N particles lead to kappa-distributed single-particle velocities as N→∞. A practical Monte Carlo Metropolis simulation in the inverse gamma ensemble is introduced for generating kappa velocities.
AI.result: The paper establishes a connection between the inverse gamma distribution of total kinetic energies and kappa-distributed single-particle velocities in the N→∞ limit, and provides a practical numerical method (Monte Carlo Metropolis in the inverse gamma ensemble) to generate kappa-distributed velocities.
AI.conclusion: This work extends the superstatistical framework to a specific application, offering both theoretical insight into kappa distributions beyond nonextensive statistical mechanics and a practical simulation tool for generating them.

title: Enhancement of far-field thermal emission via polaritonic cavity modes
summary: Controlling thermal emission is crucial for applications involving thermophotovoltaics, thermal sensing, imaging, and camouflage. While prior studies focused on the emission of thermally excited guided modes (TEGMs) inside cavities, their contribution to the far-field radiation outside cavities has remained unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a tunable far-field thermal channel enabled by TEGMs arising from the coupling of surface phonon-polaritons and cavity resonances. By combining infrared emissivity experiments with fluctuational electrodynamics simulations, we identify distinct spectral features marking the conversion of two-dimensionally confined polaritonic modes into three-dimensional radiative channels. We find that silicon cavities covered with SiO2 enhance the emissivity by up to 200% near the polaritonic spectral resonance, whereas bare silicon cavities yield only broadband enhancement. These findings provide experimental evidence of TEGMs and establish a simple cavity architecture as an effective and scalable platform for tailoring thermal radiation without complex nanofabrication.

Using silicon cavities covered with SiO2, they achieve up to 200% emissivity enhancement near polaritonic resonances, establishing a simple, scalable platform for tailoring thermal radiation.

While previous work examined TEGMs inside cavities, their contribution to far-field radiation outside cavities had not been explored, leaving a gap in understanding and engineering far-field thermal channels.

They study silicon cavities, some covered with SiO2, to investigate the coupling of surface phonon-polaritons and cavity resonances, and identify spectral features indicating conversion of 2D confined polaritonic modes into 3D radiative channels.

Distinct spectral features mark the conversion of two-dimensionally confined polaritonic modes into three-dimensional radiative channels.
AI.conclusion: The work provides experimental evidence of TEGMs contributing to far-field radiation and establishes a simple cavity architecture as an effective, scalable platform for tailoring thermal radiation without requiring complex nanofabrication.

title: Alloy engineering of excitonic properties in TMD monolayers
summary: We investigate monolayer MoS$_{2x}$Se$_{2(1-x)}$ alloys across the full composition range using optical spectroscopy. We demonstrate continuous tuning of the optical gap over $\sim$0.35 eV, accompanied by a systematic reduction of the B--A exciton splitting, in agreement with density functional theory calculations. Temperature-dependent measurements reveal a progressive increase of the average phonon energy from Se-rich to S-rich alloys that follows a simple reduced-mass scaling model. Polarization-resolved spectroscopy further shows a monotonic increase of the circular polarization from nearly zero in MoSe$_2$ to $\sim$15\% in MoS$_2$ at 78 K. The observed evolution of the polarization is attributed to alloy-induced modifications of the electronic structure that modify bright--dark exciton mixing and the associated valley depolarization. These findings establish alloy engineering as an effective strategy for controlling excitonic properties in TMD monolayers.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates monolayer MoS₂ₓSe₂₍₁₋ₓ₎ alloys across the full composition range using optical spectroscopy, demonstrating tunable optical gaps, systematic exciton splitting reduction, composition-dependent phonon energies, and alloy-induced modulation of circular polarization in transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers.
AI.motivation: To establish alloy engineering as a viable strategy for controlling excitonic properties in TMD monolayers by understanding how composition affects optical, vibrational, and valley-selective properties.
AI.method: Optical spectroscopy across the full composition range of monolayer MoS₂ₓSe₂₍₁₋ₓ₎ alloys, including temperature-dependent measurements, polarization-resolved spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations.
AI.result: Continuous tuning of the optical gap over ~0.35 eV; systematic reduction of B-A exciton splitting; progressive increase of average phonon energy from Se-rich to S-rich alloys following a reduced-mass scaling model; monotonic increase of circular polarization from nearly zero in MoSe₂ to ~15% in MoS₂ at 78 K.
AI.conclusion: Alloy engineering is an effective strategy for controlling excitonic properties in TMD monolayers, with composition-induced electronic structure modifications governing bright-dark exciton mixing and valley depolarization.

title: TNASS: Tensor Network Active Space Selection with the Entanglement Feature
summary: The quality of multi-scale modelling techniques in molecular electronic structure calculations, such as embedding and subspace methods, relies upon the chosen active space. The automation of active space selection is vital for ensuring the accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability in such calculations. In this work, we introduce Tensor Network Active Space Selection using the Entanglement Feature. Through the isolation of strongly correlated electrons, this method provides a scalable foundation for embedding methods in multi-scale modelling. By representing the purities of all possible orbital partitions as a Matrix Product State, our method isolates regions of strong electron correlation without requiring manual preselection of target atoms or the calculation of expensive high-order density matrices. The results demonstrate that this approach leads to lower ground state energies and more accurate dipole moments than other fully automated selection schemes such as those based solely on single-orbital entropy or the selection of spatial orbitals around the HOMO/LUMO gap.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Tensor Network Active Space Selection using the Entanglement Feature (TN-ASEF), a fully automated method for selecting active spaces in multi-scale molecular electronic structure calculations. By representing the purities of all possible orbital partitions as a Matrix Product State, the method isolates strongly correlated electrons without manual preselection of target atoms or expensive high-order density matrices, achieving lower ground state energies and more accurate dipole moments than existing automated schemes.
AI.motivation: Active space selection is critical for the quality of multi-scale modelling techniques such as embedding and subspace methods in molecular electronic structure calculations. Manual preselection of active spaces is error-prone, non-reproducible, and not scalable, creating a need for automated, accurate, and scalable selection methods.
AI.method: The method, Tensor Network Active Space Selection using the Entanglement Feature (TN-ASEF), represents the purities of all possible orbital partitions as a Matrix Product State (MPS). This tensor network representation allows the identification of strongly correlated orbital regions by isolating strongly correlated electrons, without requiring manual target atom preselection or computation of expensive high-order density matrices.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves lower ground state energies and more accurate dipole moments compared to other fully automated selection schemes, including those based solely on single-orbital entropy and selection of spatial orbitals around the HOMO/LUMO gap.
AI.conclusion: TN-ASEF provides a scalable and fully automated foundation for active space selection in embedding and subspace methods, improving the accuracy and reproducibility of multi-scale molecular electronic structure calculations.

title: Manipulation of localized excitons in CrPS$_4$ by temperature and magnetic field
summary: Layered van der Waals magnetic semiconductors provide a versatile platform for exploring excitonic phenomena intertwined with spin and lattice degrees of freedom, enabling excitons to act as sensitive probes of magnetic order. CrPS$_4$ is a layered antiferromagnetic semiconductor that hosts rich excitonic features whose microscopic origin and connection to magnetic ordering remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the electronic and excitonic properties of bulk CrPS$_4$ using a combination of many-body perturbation theory, dynamical mean-field theory, and photoluminescence-based experiments. Our calculations establish CrPS$_4$ as a direct-gap semiconductor with a bandgap of 2.48~eV in the antiferromagnetic phase. Several sub-bandgap excitonic transitions are predicted by theory, comprising multiple spin-allowed excitons and an additional spin-flip excitation, predominantly localized on the Cr$^{3+}$ ions. Temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent optical measurements reveal thermally driven exciton redistribution among localized states and identify characteristic energy shifts that provide clear optical signatures of magnetic phase transitions in CrPS$_4$. These results provide new insights into the excitonic transitions of antiferromagnets and suggest potential routes for all-optical sensing and light-driven control of their magnetic order.

It establishes CrPS4 as a direct-gap semiconductor with a 2.48 eV bandgap, predicts multiple sub-bandgap excitonic transitions (including spin-allowed excitons and a spin-flip excitation localized on Cr3+ ions), and identifies characteristic energy shifts in temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent optical measurements that serve as signatures of magnetic phase transitions.

The authors aim to clarify the relationship between excitons and magnetic order in this layered antiferromagnetic semiconductor, which is important because excitons can act as sensitive probes of magnetic order in van der Waals magnetic semiconductors.
AI.method: The study combines many-body perturbation theory (GW/BSE-type approach), dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), and temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent photoluminescence experiments to jointly determine the electronic structure and excitonic spectra of bulk CrPS4.

Theory predicts multiple sub-bandgap excitonic transitions comprising spin-allowed excitons and an additional spin-flip excitation, predominantly localized on Cr3+ ions. Optical experiments reveal thermally driven exciton redistribution among localized states and characteristic energy shifts that serve as clear optical signatures of magnetic phase transitions.

title: Machine Learning Bandgap Prediction of Nanoporous Graphenes with Water
summary: The structure and dynamical behavior of water confined at or within nanostructures is a topic central to many fields, from biology to emerging electronics such as carbon nanostructures. Nanoporous graphene (NPG) containing periodic nanoscale pores with specific topologies has emerged as a promising material in carbon-based nanoelectronics; however, its interaction with ambient water remains poorly understood. Here, we combine density functional theory (DFT), ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), and interpretable machine learning (ML) to reveal how water controls quantum transport in NPGs. Depending on the local hydration structure, the bandgap varies by more than a factor of two across NPG and nitrogen-doped hybrid (h-NPG) systems. To uncover the underlying mechanism, we develop Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP)-based black-box and physics-informed grey-box ML models. The Gaussian process regression model achieves near-DFT accuracy while enabling physical interpretation. Analysis identifies water dipole orientation, water-substrate distance, water center-of-geometry, and ribbon-resolved dipole moments as the dominant factors controlling bandgap modulation across NPG and h-NPG systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how confined water modulates quantum transport in nanoporous graphene (NPG) and nitrogen-doped hybrid (h-NPG) systems using DFT, ab initio molecular dynamics, and interpretable machine learning. The bandgap varies by more than a factor of two depending on local hydration structure, and SOAP-based Gaussian process regression models achieving near-DFT accuracy reveal that water dipole orientation, water-substrate distance, water center-of-geometry, and ribbon-resolved dipole moments are the dominant factors controlling bandgap modulation.
AI.motivation: Water confined at or within nanostructures is central to many fields from biology to nanoelectronics, yet the interaction between ambient water and nanoporous graphene—a promising material for carbon-based nanoelectronics—remains poorly understood.
AI.method: The study combines density functional theory (DFT), ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), and interpretable machine learning. Specifically, Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP)-based black-box and physics-informed grey-box ML models are developed, with Gaussian process regression employed to achieve near-DFT accuracy while enabling physical interpretation.

The Gaussian process regression model achieves near-DFT accuracy, and the ML interpretability analysis identifies water dipole orientation, water-substrate distance, water center-of-geometry, and ribbon-resolved dipole moments as the dominant factors controlling bandgap modulation.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning combined with first-principles simulations reveals the key physical descriptors governing how water controls quantum transport in nanoporous graphene systems, providing a mechanistic understanding of water-graphene interactions relevant to carbon-based nanoelectronics.

title: Magnetic and crystal electric field excitations in a spin-orbit coupled frustrated hyperkagome magnet Nd$_3$Li$_3$W$_2$O$_{12}$
summary: Rare-earth based garnets provide a viable platform for studying the frustrated driven magnetic properties of the hyperkagome lattices. Herein, we report a comprehensive study of the magnetic properties and crystal electric field (CEF) scheme of a new Nd$^{3+}$ based hyperkagome antiferromagnet, Nd$_3$Li$_3$W$_2$O$_{12}$ belonging to the garnet family via magnetization, heat capacity, and inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements. Magnetization measurement reveals a dominant antiferromagnetic interaction with a low temperature Curie-Weiss temperature $θ_{\rm CW}^{\rm LT} \simeq -0.2$ K. Two broad maxima are observed in the magnetic heat capacity data under magnetic fields, implying multilevel Schottky anomalies due to the effect of CEF and display a two-step magnetic entropy release. No magnetic long-range order is observed down to 0.1 K. The CEF excitations of the Nd$^{3+}$ ($J=9/2$) ion with $D_2$ point group symmetry, probed via INS experiments, show non-dispersive excitations characterizing the transitions among the CEF energy levels. The simultaneous fit of the INS spectra at different temperatures enabled the mapping of the CEF Hamiltonian and the energy eigenvalues of the Kramers' doublets. The simulation using the obtained CEF parameters reproduces the experimental magnetic susceptibility, magnetic isotherms, and magnetic heat capacity data. The thermodynamic properties and INS-derived crystal-field scheme confirm a Kramers' doublet ground state with an effective spin $J_{\rm eff} = 1/2$ at low temperatures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive study of the magnetic properties and crystal electric field (CEF) scheme of Nd3Li3W2O12, a rare-earth garnet hyperkagome antiferromagnet, using magnetization, heat capacity, and inelastic neutron scattering measurements. The system exhibits dominant antiferromagnetic interactions with a low Curie-Weiss temperature, multilevel Schottky anomalies, no magnetic long-range order down to 0.1 K, and a Kramers' doublet ground state with effective spin J_eff = 1/2 at low temperatures.
AI.motivation: To understand the frustrated magnetic properties of hyperkagome lattices using rare-earth garnets as a platform, and to fully characterize the crystal electric field scheme of a new Nd3+-based hyperkagome antiferromagnet, providing insight into its low-temperature magnetic behavior.
AI.method: The study combines magnetization measurements, heat capacity measurements, and inelastic neutron scattering (INS) experiments. The INS spectra at different temperatures were simultaneously fit to map the CEF Hamiltonian and energy eigenvalues of Kramers' doublets for the Nd3+ (J=9/2) ion with D2 point group symmetry.
AI.result: Magnetization reveals dominant antiferromagnetic interaction with a low-temperature Curie-Weiss temperature of approximately -0.2 K. Two broad maxima in magnetic heat capacity under magnetic fields indicate multilevel Schottky anomalies with two-step magnetic entropy release. No magnetic long-range order is observed down to 0.1 K. The CEF parameters obtained from simultaneous fits of INS spectra at different temperatures successfully reproduce experimental magnetic susceptibility, magnetic isotherms, and magnetic heat capacity data.
AI.conclusion: The thermodynamic properties and INS-derived CEF scheme confirm a Kramers' doublet ground state with an effective spin J_eff = 1/2 at low temperatures, establishing Nd3Li3W2O12 as a candidate for studying frustrated magnetism on the hyperkagome lattice without magnetic long-range order.

title: High-Order Response Functions with Duschinsky Coupling and Finite Temperature: Application to Two-Dimensional Resonance Raman Spectroscopy
summary: In this work, we derive closed-form expressions for multi-time correlation functions underlying higher-order nonlinear spectroscopic response functions within the harmonic approximation. Our method includes displacements, frequency changes, and Duschinsky rotation between the vibrational modes of different electronic states while retaining polynomial scaling with the number of degrees of freedom. Finite temperature is accounted for without summation over vibrational eigenstates. To show the capabilities of our method, we apply it to calculate fifth-order two-dimensional resonance Raman (2DRR) spectra of two-mode model systems and naphthalene. Comparison with the displaced harmonic oscillator model shows that Duschinsky rotation modifies the positions and relative intensities of diagonal and cross peaks. Overall, our results demonstrate that 2DRR spectroscopy is particularly sensitive to changes in normal coordinates between electronic states and can provide distinct signatures of Duschinsky coupling in molecular systems.

AI.tldr: This paper derives closed-form expressions for multi-time correlation functions underlying higher-order nonlinear spectroscopic response functions within the harmonic approximation, including displacements, frequency changes, and Duschinsky rotation, with polynomial scaling and finite temperature treatment. Applied to fifth-order two-dimensional resonance Raman spectra of model systems and naphthalene, the results show 2DRR spectroscopy is sensitive to normal coordinate changes between electronic states, providing distinct signatures of Duschinsky coupling.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient method for computing higher-order nonlinear spectroscopic response functions that include realistic vibrational effects such as Duschinsky rotation, which are computationally challenging and not captured by simpler displaced harmonic oscillator models.
AI.method: Closed-form analytical expressions for multi-time correlation functions are derived within a harmonic approximation framework that incorporates displacements, frequency changes, and Duschinsky rotation between vibrational modes of different electronic states. The approach maintains polynomial scaling with the number of degrees of freedom and avoids explicit summation over vibrational eigenstates, thereby handling finite temperatures efficiently.
AI.result: The method was applied to compute fifth-order two-dimensional resonance Raman (2DRR) spectra for two-mode model systems and naphthalene. Comparison with the displaced harmonic oscillator model demonstrates that Duschinsky rotation significantly alters peak positions and relative intensities of both diagonal and cross peaks.
AI.conclusion: Two-dimensional resonance Raman spectroscopy is particularly sensitive to changes in normal coordinates between electronic states and can provide distinct experimental signatures of Duschinsky coupling in molecular systems.

title: Emergence and Detection of Surface altermagnetism in KV$_2$Se$_2$O
summary: We demonstrate the recent concept of emergent surface altermagnetism through its unique signatures in \KVSO. We show that for bulk antiferromagnetically ordered \KVSO, the (001) surface exhibits $d$-wave altermagnetism. Our results fully explain the recent seemingly contradicgting experimental evidence, independently showing both an antiferromagnetically ordered bulk from neutron diffraction, and $d$-wave spin splitting from photoemission spectroscopy. To fully verify this conecept, we predict, as a key experimental signature, a large nonlinear Edelstein response, which is localized at the surface, and follows the $d$-wave altermagnetic symmetry. These results are not only relevant for the metallic and room-temperature magnet \KVSO, but also for several other Lieb lattice systems. Our work expands the pool of techniques that can be used to detect altermagnetism emerging at the surfaces of antiferromagnets.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates emergent surface altermagnetism in the metallic room-temperature magnet KVSO, showing that the (001) surface of bulk antiferromagnetically ordered KVSO exhibits d-wave altermagnetism, which resolves conflicting experimental evidence from neutron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy. The work predicts a large nonlinear Edelstein response as a key experimental signature, extends beyond KVSO to other Lieb lattice systems, and expands techniques for detecting surface altermagnetism in antiferromagnets.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to resolve apparent contradictions in experimental observations of KVSO: neutron diffraction indicates antiferromagnetic bulk ordering while photoemission spectroscopy shows d-wave spin splitting. The authors propose emergent surface altermagnetism as the unifying concept to explain both observations and provide a framework to verify this concept.
AI.method: The authors theoretically demonstrate emergent surface altermagnetism in the (001) surface of bulk antiferromagnetically ordered KVSO. They analyze the d-wave altermagnetic character of the surface and predict a nonlinear Edelstein response that is surface-localized and follows the d-wave altermagnetic symmetry, serving as a distinct experimental signature.
AI.result: The study fully explains both seemingly contradictory experimental results—antiferromagnetic bulk ordering (neutron diffraction) and d-wave spin splitting (photoemission)—as a consequence of emergent surface altermagnetism. A large nonlinear Edelstein response localized at the surface with d-wave symmetry is predicted as a key verification signature, with relevance extended to other Lieb lattice systems.
AI.conclusion: Emergent surface altermagnetism is established in KVSO as a valid concept reconciling prior experiments. The predicted nonlinear Edelstein effect provides a new experimental technique for detecting altermagnetism at antiferromagnet surfaces, broadening the toolkit beyond existing methods and potentially applicable to other Lieb lattice materials.

title: Controllable interaction between photons and distant spins via vacuum Rabi oscillations
summary: Vacuum Rabi oscillations between a single photon and a single spin demonstrate the capability of harnessing light-matter interaction at the level of a single quantum of energy. Since the observation of strong spin-photon coupling in gate-defined quantum dots, probing this interaction in the time-domain has been a major objective. Here, we carefully engineer a device composed of two spatially separated double quantum dots hosting single electron spin qubits and a superconducting cavity to accommodate microwave photons. We observe multiple vacuum Rabi oscillations between each spin qubit and the cavity. By concatenating vacuum Rabi oscillations involving the two spins, an energy excitation in one qubit can be emitted as a photon and then transferred to the other qubit. When a single photon is emitted, the cavity is prepared in a Fock state, leading to an accelerated vacuum Rabi frequency. These results serve as building blocks not only in exploring light-matter interactions, but also in interfacing semiconductor spin qubits to photonic links.

AI.tldr: The authors engineer a device coupling two spatially separated double quantum dot spin qubits to a superconducting microwave cavity, observing multiple vacuum Rabi oscillations between each spin and the cavity. They demonstrate coherent transfer of a single excitation from one qubit to another via a cavity photon, and prepare the cavity in a Fock state that accelerates the vacuum Rabi frequency.
AI.motivation: Since the discovery of strong spin-photon coupling in gate-defined quantum dots, probing this interaction in the time-domain has been a major goal. Observing vacuum Rabi oscillations between a single spin and a single photon would provide fundamental insight into light-matter interaction at the single-quantum level and lay groundwork for interfacing spin qubits with photonic links.
AI.method: The device consists of two spatially separated double quantum dots, each hosting a single electron spin qubit, coupled to a superconducting cavity for microwave photons. The system is carefully engineered to achieve strong spin-photon coupling, enabling time-domain observation of vacuum Rabi oscillations. By concatenating Rabi oscillations involving both spins, an excitation in one qubit is emitted as a photon and transferred to the other qubit.
AI.result: Multiple vacuum Rabi oscillations are observed between each spin qubit and the cavity. Coherent energy transfer between two distant spin qubits via a cavity photon is demonstrated. When a single photon is emitted, the cavity is prepared in a Fock state, which leads to an accelerated vacuum Rabi frequency.
AI.conclusion: These results provide building blocks for exploring light-matter interactions at the single-quantum level and for interfacing semiconductor spin qubits with photonic links, enabling scalable quantum information processing.

title: Anisotropic Phonon Heat Flow and Thermoelectric Response in Tetragonal GeS$_2$ and GeSe$_2$
comment: 31 pages, 25 figures, and 6 tables. Includes supplementary information
summary:
The electronic structure, lattice dynamics, bonding, elastic response, and anisotropic thermoelectric transport properties of tetragonal GeS$_2$ and GeSe$_2$ were investigated using density functional theory, density functional perturbation theory, Wannier interpolation, and scattering-aware Boltzmann transport. The relaxed structures are mechanically and dynamically stable within the calculated harmonic description. The HSE03/Wannier band gaps are 2.48 eV for GeS$_2$ and 1.23 eV for GeSe$_2$, while substitution of S by Se lowers the upper phonon frequency from approximately 13.6 to 10.3 THz.
  The phonon Boltzmann transport calculations reveal pronounced lattice-transport anisotropy. Within the relaxation-time approximation, the 300 K in-plane and cross-plane lattice thermal conductivities are 26.86 and 1.19 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ for GeS$_2$, and 18.74 and 1.52 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ for GeSe$_2$, respectively. At 800 K, these values decrease to 10.22 and 0.46 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ for GeS$_2$, and 7.25 and 0.58 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ for GeSe$_2$. Frequency-resolved analysis shows that low-frequency phonons carry most of the heat, whereas the small cross-plane values reflect restricted out-of-plane phonon transport.
  Combining the ShengBTE RTA lattice tensors with AMSET electronic coefficients gives $zT=0.257$ for n-type cross-plane GeS$_2$ at 800 K and $10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$. The corresponding PBE-AMSET estimate for GeSe$_2$ is $zT=0.066$ for p-type cross-plane transport at 800 K and $3\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$. LOBSTER analysis identifies mixed covalent--ionic Ge--X bonding, with Ge--S bonds having a larger stabilizing ICOHP magnitude than Ge--Se bonds ($-5.27$ versus $-4.74$ eV per bond). These results identify tetragonal GeX$_2$ compounds as strongly anisotropic thermoelectrics with moderate calculated $zT$ values whose cross-plane response benefits from suppressed lattice heat transport.

AI.tldr: The paper uses first-principles methods (DFT, DFPT, Wannier interpolation, scattering-aware Boltzmann transport) to study the electronic structure, lattice dynamics, bonding, elastic response, and thermoelectric transport of tetragonal GeS₂ and GeSe₂. They find strongly anisotropic lattice thermal conductivities (in-plane ~19-27 W/m·K vs cross-plane ~1.2-1.5 W/m·K at 300 K), yielding moderate zT values of 0.257 (n-type cross-plane GeS₂ at 800 K) and 0.066 (p-type cross-plane GeSe₂ at 800 K).
AI.motivation: To characterize tetragonal GeX₂ (X = S, Se) compounds as potential thermoelectric materials, with emphasis on understanding their anisotropic transport properties and whether suppressed cross-plane lattice thermal conductivity can enhance thermoelectric performance.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT), density functional perturbation theory (DFPT), Wannier interpolation (HSE03/Wannier for band gaps, PBE-AMSET for electronic transport), scattering-aware Boltzmann transport (ShengBTE RTA for lattice thermal conductivity, AMSET for electronic coefficients), and LOBSTER analysis for chemical bonding (ICOHP).
